Under such a setting, we demonstrate various error modes where an attention model can be accurate but fail to be interpretable, and show that such models do occur as a result of training. We illustrate various situations that can accentuate and mitigate this behaviour. Finally, we use our objective definition of interpretability for SDC tasks to evaluate a few attention model learning algorithms designed to encourage sparsity and demonstrate that these algorithms help improve interpretability.

papers.title: Warp: a method for neural network interpretability applied to gene expression profiles
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be interpreted in the context of gene expression analysis to recover meaningful information on a sample-specific basis?
papers.core_contribution: Warping is a method for neural network interpretability that recovers sample-specific gene signatures by interpolating in input or representation space, demonstrating effectiveness on linearly and non-linearly separable datasets.
papers.conclusion: Warping shows promise as a flexible method for post-hoc interpretation of neural networks in computational biology, enabling the examination of class gene signatures with sample-specific insights.
papers.key_findings:
Warping works well on non-linearly separable datasets like XOR, allowing data points to migrate across decision boundaries.
The method provides sample-specific bias vectors, highlighting individual adjustments needed for classification changes.
In a VAE-based approach, warping recovers biologically meaningful gene expression adjustments, such as suppressing surfactant genes and boosting kidney-specific genes to change phenotype classification.
papers.limitation:
Linear interpolation assumes the data manifold is continuous in input space, which may lead to adversarial examples.
Reconstruction blurriness caused by the variational autoencoder encoding.
future_direction: Determine how destructive warps are to other gene signatures within samples.
Overcome reconstruction blurriness caused by the VAE encoding.
papers.abstract: We show a proof of principle for warping, a method to interpret the inner working of neural networks in the context of gene expression analysis. Warping is an efficient way to gain insight to the inner workings of neural nets and make them more interpretable. We demonstrate the ability of warping to recover meaningful information for a given class on a samplespecific individual basis. We found warping works well in both linearly and nonlinearly separable datasets. These encouraging results show that warping has a potential to be the answer to neural networks interpretability in computational biology.

papers.title: DoLFIn: Distributions over Latent Features for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we achieve interpretability in neural models without sacrificing accuracy by using probability distributions over latent features?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DoLFIn, a novel architecture for interpretability that uses probability distributions over latent features, and shows it achieves comparable or better accuracy than baselines while providing interpretability.
papers.conclusion: DoLFIn provides a new way to build explainable models without sacrificing accuracy, and it offers better interpretability than attention and saliency maps.
papers.key_findings:
DoLFIn achieves slightly higher accuracy than CNN and BiLSTM on SST2 and AG-news datasets.
DoLFIn provides interpretability by computing the probability that an input word supports a category, which is more informative than attention or saliency maps.
The latent features in DoLFIn can be analyzed to understand which categories they support, and some features are more specific to certain categories.
papers.limitation: The analysis of the meaning of latent features is only done on a cherry-picked example and deeper analysis is left for future work.
future_direction: Deeply analyzing the meaning of latent features.
papers.abstract: Interpreting the inner workings of neural models is a key step in ensuring the robustness and trustworthiness of the models, but work on neural network interpretability typically faces a trade-off: either the models are too constrained to be very useful, or the solutions found by the models are too complex to interpret. We propose a novel strategy for achieving interpretability that -- in our experiments -- avoids this trade-off. Our approach builds on the success of using probability as the central quantity, such as for instance within the attention mechanism. In our architecture, DoLFIn (Distributions over Latent Features for Interpretability), we do no determine beforehand what each feature represents, and features go altogether into an unordered set. Each feature has an associated probability ranging from 0 to 1, weighing its importance for further processing. We show that, unlike attention and saliency map approaches, this set-up makes it straight-forward to compute the probability with which an input component supports the decision the neural model makes. To demonstrate the usefulness of the approach, we apply DoLFIn to text classification, and show that DoLFIn not only provides interpretable solutions, but even slightly outperforms the classical CNN and BiLSTM text classifiers on the SST2 and AG-news datasets.

papers.title: DGTN: Graph-Enhanced Transformer with Diffusive Attention Gating Mechanism for Enzyme DDG Prediction
papers.research_question: How can we accurately predict the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (∆∆G) by integrating sequence and structural information through a co-learning framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DGTN, a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network and transformer representations through a bidirectional diffusion mechanism for protein stability prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: DGTN effectively integrates 3D geometric and evolutionary sequence context through bidirectional diffusion, establishing a principled and interpretable paradigm for accurate protein stability prediction and design.
papers.key_findings:
DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance on ProTherm with Pearson correlation ρ=0.87 and RMSE=1.21 kcal/mol, outperforming existing baselines.
Ablation studies show the bidirectional diffusion mechanism contributes a 6-point gain in Pearson correlation over simple cross-modal fusion.
The model generalizes well to unseen datasets (SKEMPI, Ssym, FireProtDB), demonstrating robust learning of stability principles.
Theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to an optimal structure-aware attention matrix with a convergence rate of O(1/√T).
Attention visualization confirms the model successfully identifies spatially proximate but sequentially distant residue interactions.
papers.limitation:
Operates on a single static conformation of the wild-type protein, unable to capture dynamic or entropic contributions to stability.
Evaluates mutations in isolation and does not explicitly model epistatic (non-additive) interactions between multiple substitutions.
Training data (ProTherm) exhibits class imbalance, with certain protein families overrepresented, potentially limiting generalization.
future_direction: Incorporate ensembles of structures (from molecular dynamics or predicted distributions) to model flexibility and allostery.
Extend the architecture to jointly represent combinatorial mutations via graph-based mutation encoding or interaction-aware attention.
Improve robustness to dataset imbalance via domain-adversarial training, balanced sampling, or cross-family transfer learning.
papers.abstract: Predicting the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (DDG) is fundamental to protein engineering and drug design. While recent deep learning approaches have shown promise, they often process sequence and structure information independently, failing to capture the intricate coupling between local structural geometry and global sequential patterns. We present DGTN (Diffused Graph-Transformer Network), a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network (GNN) weights for structural priors and transformer attention through a diffusion mechanism. Our key innovation is a bidirectional diffusion process where: (1) GNN-derived structural embeddings guide transformer attention via learnable diffusion kernels, and (2) transformer representations refine GNN message passing through attention-modulated graph updates. We provide rigorous mathematical analysis showing this co-learning scheme achieves provably better approximation bounds than independent processing. On ProTherm and SKEMPI benchmarks, DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance (Pearson Rho = 0.87, RMSE = 1.21 kcal/mol), with 6.2% improvement over best baselines. Ablation studies confirm the diffusion mechanism contributes 4.8 points to correlation. Our theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to optimal structure-sequence coupling, with convergence rate O(1/sqrt(T) ) where T is diffusion steps. This work establishes a principled framework for integrating heterogeneous protein representations through learnable diffusion.

papers.title: Interpretability in Linear Brain Decoding
papers.research_question: What is a formal definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models, and how can we quantitatively evaluate interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a formal definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models and proposes a multi-objective criterion combining interpretability and performance for model selection.
papers.conclusion: The proposed definition provides a theoretical background for the quantitative evaluation of interpretability in linear brain decoding.
papers.key_findings:
In noisy data, the most accurate linear decoding model is not necessarily the most interpretable, highlighting a trade-off between performance and interpretability.
Incorporating the proposed interpretability measure into model selection can lead to more interpretable models when using regularization techniques like Lasso.
papers.limitation:
The definition of interpretability is theoretical and assumes the true solution of the brain decoding problem is available, which is not realistic in practice.
The definition and quantification are limited to linear models; extending to non-linear models requires future research.
future_direction: Extending the definition of interpretability to non-linear models.
papers.abstract: Improving the interpretability of brain decoding approaches is of primary interest in many neuroimaging studies. Despite extensive studies of this type, at present, there is no formal definition for interpretability of brain decoding models. As a consequence, there is no quantitative measure for evaluating the interpretability of different brain decoding methods. In this paper, we present a simple definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models. Then, we propose to combine the interpretability and the performance of the brain decoding into a new multi-objective criterion for model selection. Our preliminary results on the toy data show that optimizing the hyper-parameters of the regularized linear classifier based on the proposed criterion results in more informative linear models. The presented definition provides the theoretical background for quantitative evaluation of interpretability in linear brain decoding.

papers.title: T3-Vis: visual analytic for Training and fine-Tuning Transformers in NLP
papers.research_question: How can we design a visual analytic framework to assist researchers in understanding and interpreting the training and fine-tuning processes of Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents T3-Vis, a visual analytic framework that integrates multiple interactive visualizations to help researchers understand and interpret the training and fine-tuning of Transformer models by providing insights into hidden states, attention patterns, and training dynamics.
papers.conclusion: T3-Vis is an effective framework for interpreting Transformer models during training and fine-tuning, and it helps identify potential directions to improve task performance.
papers.key_findings:
In extractive summarization, important attention heads exhibit patterns where tokens attend to other tokens of the same word, tokens within the same sentence, and adjacent tokens.
In topic classification, the framework helped identify misclassified examples and revealed that the model sometimes focuses on unimportant details or fails when background knowledge is required.
The framework was found useful by researchers in a focus group for interpreting model behavior and identifying potential improvements.
papers.limitation:
The interface is more useful for classification problems with well-defined evaluation metrics.
There is information loss intrinsic in the dimension reduction methods used for visualization.
The front-end needs optimization to support visualization of large-scale datasets.
future_direction: Extend the framework to provide more advanced visualization for custom Transformers, such as models with more complex connections (e.g., parallel attention layers) or advanced attention mechanisms (e.g., sparse attention).
papers.abstract: Transformers are the dominant architecture in NLP, but their training and fine-tuning is still very challenging. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of a visual analytic framework for assisting researchers in such process, by providing them with valuable insights about the model's intrinsic properties and behaviours. Our framework offers an intuitive overview that allows the user to explore different facets of the model (e.g., hidden states, attention) through interactive visualization, and allows a suite of built-in algorithms that compute the importance of model components and different parts of the input sequence. Case studies and feedback from a user focus group indicate that the framework is useful, and suggest several improvements. Our framework is available at:

papers.title: Effective Attention Sheds Light On Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does effective attention provide different interpretations than standard attention for transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Effective attention, which contributes to model output, reveals different interpretations than standard attention, being less focused on delimiter tokens and more on task-relevant linguistic features.
papers.conclusion: Effective attention should be used for interpreting transformers as it is more pertinent to model output and reveals task-relevant features.
papers.key_findings:
Effective attention shows fewer vertical patterns associated with delimiter tokens compared to standard attention.
Effective attention disregards [SEP] and punctuation tokens but not [CLS].
Effective attention highlights end-task linguistic features instead of pretraining-related features.
Changes in attention due to fine-tuning are captured by effective attention, confirming its relevance to model output.
Effective attention is more pertinent for interpreting transformer behavior as it directly contributes to the output.
papers.limitation: Effective attention is slower to compute due to the SVD decomposition, which can be a bottleneck for large-scale analyses.
future_direction: A more formal study comparing norm-based analysis and effective attention.
papers.abstract: An attention matrix of a transformer selfattention sublayer can provably be decomposed into two components and only one of them (effective attention) contributes to the model output. This leads us to ask whether visualizing effective attention gives different conclusions than interpretation of standard attention. Using a subset of the GLUE tasks and BERT, we carry out an analysis to compare the two attention matrices, and show that their interpretations differ. Effective attention is less associated with the features related to the language modeling pretraining such as the separator token, and it has more potential to illustrate linguistic features captured by the model for solving the end-task. Given the found differences, we recommend using effective attention for studying a transformer's behavior since it is more pertinent to the model output by design.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformers Models
papers.research_question: How to interactively explore and understand what attention heads in transformer models have learned, specifically in BERT, by combining attention visualization with nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to explore and explain learned representations and attention mechanisms in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to reveal intelligible structure in learned representations of transformer models, demonstrated with BERT on the Wizard of Oz corpus.
papers.key_findings:
At early layers (e.g., layer 1), masked token embeddings show similarity to common tokens like punctuation and determinants, with no meaningful linguistic information encoded.
As layers progress, more part-of-speech information is added; by layer 6, BERT becomes confident that a masked token is a verb, refining this estimation in later layers.
Complex dependencies such as direct object (DOBJ) are detected in early-middle layers but rely on a combination of multiple attention heads, not individual heads.
Positional heads attend to succeeding or preceding tokens and encode linguistic information about the attended-to word, such as part-of-speech and dependency relations.
EXBERT enables interactive exploration of how attention heads contribute to encoding linguistic features in token embeddings through nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce powerful contextual representations that lead to improvements across many NLP tasks. Since these models are typically guided by a sequence of learned self attention mechanisms and may comprise undesired inductive biases, it is paramount to be able to explore what the attention has learned. While static analyses of these models lead to targeted insights, interactive tools are more dynamic and can help humans better gain an intuition for the model-internal reasoning process. We present exBERT, an interactive tool named after the popular BERT language model, that provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations by matching a human-specified input to similar contexts in a large annotated dataset. By aggregating the annotations of the matching similar contexts, exBERT helps intuitively explain what each attention-head has learned.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: From Neurons to Neutrons: A Case Study in Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability extract scientific knowledge from neural networks trained on physics data, and can such insights align with human-derived domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can extract scientifically meaningful representations from neural networks trained on nuclear physics data, aligning with human-derived concepts like the semi-empirical mass formula and shell model.
papers.conclusion: These findings provide a proof-of-concept that neural networks, when trained on scientific data, can learn useful representations that align with human knowledge, opening exciting possibilities for future research on richer data and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings of proton and neutron numbers exhibit a helix structure that encodes nuclear physics concepts like the volume and asymmetry terms.
The orderedness of embeddings along the first principal component correlates with generalization performance.
Penultimate layer features correspond to terms in the semi-empirical mass formula and nuclear shell model.
Latent space topography reveals the algorithm used by the model for binding energy prediction, geometrically representing the SEMF.
Models trained on nuclear data learn representations similar to those trained on pseudo data from human-derived theory.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted knowledge is not guaranteed; representations may be complex and not easily distilled into interpretable theories.
Lack of quantitative metrics to assess interpretability.
Symbolic regression from neural features did not yield fully interpretable improvements over human-derived models.
Requires interdisciplinary collaborations and close partnerships between machine learning researchers and domain experts.
future_direction: Applying interpretability to richer data and more complex tasks.
Developing quantitative metrics for interpretability.
Exploring other scientific domains for knowledge extraction.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) promises a path toward fully understanding how neural networks make their predictions. Prior work demonstrates that even when trained to perform simple arithmetic, models can implement a variety of algorithms (sometimes concurrently) depending on initialization and hyperparameters. Does this mean neuron-level interpretability techniques have limited applicability? We argue that high-dimensional neural networks can learn low-dimensional representations of their training data that are useful beyond simply making good predictions. Such representations can be understood through the mechanistic interpretability lens and provide insights that are surprisingly faithful to human-derived domain knowledge. This indicates that such approaches to interpretability can be useful for deriving a new understanding of a problem from models trained to solve it. As a case study, we extract nuclear physics concepts by studying models trained to reproduce nuclear data.

papers.title: Decomposing MLP Activations into Interpretable Features via Semi-Nonnegative Matrix Factorization
papers.research_question: How can we find interpretable features in large language models by decomposing MLP activations using semi-nonnegative matrix factorization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SNMF for decomposing MLP activations into interpretable features, outperforming SAEs and supervised baselines in causal steering, and reveals hierarchical structure in MLP activation space.
papers.conclusion: SNMF is a simple and effective tool for identifying interpretable features and dissecting concept representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SNMF-derived features outperform SAEs and a supervised baseline (difference-in-means) on causal steering.
SNMF features align with human-interpretable concepts and show good concept detection.
Recursive SNMF reveals hierarchical merging of features, e.g., fine-grained concepts into high-level ones.
Specific neuron combinations are reused across semantically-related features.
MLP features are compositional and exhibit a parts-based decomposition.
papers.limitation: A minority of MLP features receive negative scores, indicating they respond more strongly to neutral contexts, possibly reflecting sensitivity to noise or layer-specific biases.
future_direction: Optimizations for SNMF initialization and training
papers.abstract: A central goal for mechanistic interpretability has been to identify the right units of analysis in large language models (LLMs) that causally explain their outputs. While early work focused on individual neurons, evidence that neurons often encode multiple concepts has motivated a shift toward analyzing directions in activation space. A key question is how to find directions that capture interpretable features in an unsupervised manner. Current methods rely on dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders (SAEs), commonly trained over residual stream activations to learn directions from scratch. However, SAEs often struggle in causal evaluations and lack intrinsic interpretability, as their learning is not explicitly tied to the computations of the model. Here, we tackle these limitations by directly decomposing MLP activations with semi-nonnegative matrix factorization (SNMF), such that the learned features are (a) sparse linear combinations of co-activated neurons, and (b) mapped to their activating inputs, making them directly interpretable. Experiments on Llama 3.1, Gemma 2 and GPT-2 show that SNMF derived features outperform SAEs and a strong supervised baseline (difference-in-means) on causal steering, while aligning with human-interpretable concepts. Further analysis reveals that specific neuron combinations are reused across semantically-related features, exposing a hierarchical structure in the MLP's activation space. Together, these results position SNMF as a simple and effective tool for identifying interpretable features and dissecting concept representations in LLMs.

papers.title: Probing for Predicate Argument Structures in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: Do pretrained language models (PLMs) encode the argument structure of a predicate in its contextual representation? How are predicate senses and their argument structures encoded across layers, and how do they differ between verbal and nominal predicates and across languages?
papers.core_contribution: PLMs encode predicate argument structures in their contextual representations, with senses and rolesets encoded at different layers, and verbal and nominal predicates are represented differently. Integrating this knowledge improves SRL performance.
papers.conclusion: Probing PLMs for predicate argument structures reveals how they encode semantic information and provides insights that can be used to improve SRL systems.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs encode predicate argument structures directly into the contextualized representation of a predicate.
Predicate senses and their argument structures are encoded at different layers in PLMs.
Verbal and nominal predicate argument structures are represented differently across the layers of a PLM, making transfer between them non-trivial.
Multilingual PLMs encode predicate argument structure information similarly across English and Chinese.
Integrating predicate-argument structure knowledge into an SRL model via weighted averaging of layers and multi-task learning improves performance.
future_direction: cross-lingual transfer learning for SRL
using all layers of PLMs for SRL
papers.abstract: Thanks to the effectiveness and wide availability of modern pretrained language models (PLMs), recently proposed approaches have achieved remarkable results in dependencyand span-based, multilingual and cross-lingual Semantic Role Labeling (SRL). These results have prompted researchers to investigate the inner workings of modern PLMs with the aim of understanding how, where, and to what extent they encode information about SRL. In this paper, we follow this line of research and probe for predicate argument structures in PLMs. Our study shows that PLMs do encode semantic structures directly into the contextualized representation of a predicate, and also provides insights into the correlation between predicate senses and their structures, the degree of transferability between nominal and verbal structures, and how such structures are encoded across languages. Finally, we look at the practical implications of such insights and demonstrate the benefits of embedding predicate argument structure information into an SRL model.

papers.title: Enhancing Pre-trained Representation Classifiability can Boost its Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can classifiability-oriented pre-trained representations achieve high interpretability and classifiability simultaneously?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a positive correlation between interpretability and classifiability in pre-trained vision representations, introduces the Inherent Interpretability Score (IIS) to quantify representation interpretability, and shows that improving one can mutually promote the other.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability and classifiability are mutually promoting for classifiability-oriented pre-trained representations, allowing practitioners to unify improvements in both aspects for vision models.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability and classifiability of pre-trained representations are positively correlated, not conflicting.
Representations with higher classifiability contain more interpretable semantics that can be captured in interpretations.
Fine-tuning pre-trained models with an interpretability maximization objective (simplified IIS) can further improve their classifiability on downstream tasks.
Predictions based on the interpretations of high-classifiability representations suffer less accuracy degradation compared to the original representations.
The mutual promoting relationship provides a new pathway for interpretable representation learning.
papers.limitation:
Investigations of the underlying mechanism leading to the positive correlation between interpretability and classifiability have not been conducted.
The method fine-tunes representations by maximizing a simplified version of IIS, not the original IIS.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying mechanisms of the observed positive correlation between interpretability and classifiability.
Better integrate the Inherent Interpretability Score (IIS) into the training process of pre-trained models.
papers.abstract: The visual representation of a pre-trained model prioritizes the classifiability on downstream tasks, while the widespread applications for pre-trained visual models have posed new requirements for representation interpretability. However, it remains unclear whether the pre-trained representations can achieve high interpretability and classifiability simultaneously. To answer this question, we quantify the representation interpretability by leveraging its correlation with the ratio of interpretable semantics within the representations. Given the pre-trained representations, only the interpretable semantics can be captured by interpretations, whereas the uninterpretable part leads to information loss. Based on this fact, we propose the Inherent Interpretability Score (IIS) that evaluates the information loss, measures the ratio of interpretable semantics, and quantifies the representation interpretability. In the evaluation of the representation interpretability with different classifiability, we surprisingly discover that the interpretability and classifiability are positively correlated, i.e., representations with higher classifiability provide more interpretable semantics that can be captured in the interpretations. This observation further supports two benefits to the pre-trained representations. First, the classifiability of representations can be further improved by fine-tuning with interpretability maximization. Second, with the classifiability improvement for the representations, we obtain predictions based on their interpretations with less accuracy degradation. The discovered positive correlation and corresponding applications show that practitioners can unify the improvements in interpretability and classifiability for pre-trained vision models. Codes are available at https://github.com/ssfgunner/IIS.

papers.title: Attention network for predicting T-cell receptor–peptide binding can associate attention with interpretable protein structural properties
papers.research_question: Can an attention-based neural network accurately predict TCR-pMHC interactions and provide interpretable biological insights into TCR function and CDR3-peptide binding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a cross-attention based model (cross-TCR-interpreter) for predicting TCR-peptide binding, which achieves competitive performance and provides interpretable insights by associating attention weights with protein structural properties such as hydrogen bonds.
papers.conclusion: The study presents a computational approach for predicting TCR binding to specific ligand peptides using a cross-attention mechanism, and by analyzing protein structures, it gains new insights into TCR-peptide functional relationships.
papers.key_findings:
The cross-TCR-interpreter model achieves competitive performance on benchmark datasets for TCR-peptide binding prediction.
The model's attention weights can be statistically associated with structural properties, showing that largely attended residues are more likely to form hydrogen bonds within CDR3s.
The model struggles to generalize to unseen peptides, as evidenced by poor performance on the COVID-19 dataset and recent data test set.
Input perturbation analysis shows that altering attended residues can significantly change predictions, indicating the importance of these residues.
The attention mechanism provides interpretable insights into the binding mechanism, suggesting that internal hydrogen bonds within CDR3s may stabilize binding conformations.
papers.limitation:
The model's performance on unseen peptides is poor, as shown in the COVID-19 dataset and recent data test set.
The simplified focus on CDR3 regions might miss integral information from the complete TCR and MHC, potentially overlooking critical interactions.
The interpretability of attention values might be influenced by the imbalance in the dataset, with more TCR samples than peptide samples.
future_direction: Using different machine learning models such as meaningful perturbation methods on exhaustively collected sequences.
Incorporating more comprehensive methods like molecular simulations for a fuller view of the binding mechanism.
Improving generalization to unseen peptides by addressing dataset limitations.
papers.abstract: Understanding how a T-cell receptor (TCR) recognizes its specific ligand peptide is crucial for gaining an insight into biological functions and disease mechanisms. Despite its importance, experimentally determining TCR-peptide-major histocompatibility complex (TCR-pMHC) interactions is expensive and time-consuming. To address this challenge, computational methods have been proposed, but they are typically evaluated by internal retrospective validation only, and few researchers have incorporated and tested an attention layer from language models into structural information. Therefore, in this study, we developed a machine learning model based on a modified version of Transformer, a source-target attention neural network, to predict the TCR-pMHC interaction solely from the amino acid sequences of the TCR complementarity-determining region (CDR) 3 and the peptide. This model achieved competitive performance on a benchmark dataset of the TCR-pMHC interaction, as well as on a truly new external dataset. Additionally, by analyzing the results of binding predictions, we associated the neural network weights with protein structural properties. By classifying the residues into large- and small-attention groups, we identified statistically significant properties associated with the largely attended residues such as hydrogen bonds within CDR3. The dataset that we created and the ability of our model to provide an interpretable prediction of TCR-peptide binding should increase our knowledge about molecular recognition and pave the way for designing new therapeutics.

papers.title: CAST: Compositional Analysis via Spectral Tracking for Understanding Transformer Layer Functions
papers.research_question: How do transformer layers process information and what are their computational roles? The paper investigates internal mechanisms of transformers through transformation-centric analysis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CAST, a probe-free framework for analyzing transformer layer functions via direct transformation matrix estimation and spectral analysis, revealing distinct architectural patterns between encoder and decoder models.
papers.conclusion: CAST provides transformation-centric insights into transformer layer functions, revealing architectural patterns and offering practical guidance for model design, pruning, and training optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Decoder-only models (GPT-2, Llama, DeepSeek-R1) exhibit compression-expansion cycles through their layers, with effective rank dropping at middle layers before recovering.
Encoder-only models (RoBERTa) maintain high effective rank throughout their depth, preserving comprehensive representations.
Kernel analysis (CKA) partitions layers into three functional phases: feature extraction, compression, and specialization.
Middle compression layers in decoders exhibit the strongest nonlinearity, suggesting complex transformations during abstraction.
The linear approximation captures substantial transformation behavior, as validated by residual norm analysis.
papers.limitation:
The linear approximation may not capture all nonlinear dynamics of transformer layers.
The analysis is limited to four representative architectures; generalizability to emerging transformer variants requires further investigation.
Spectral analysis provides insights into transformation structure but does not directly address semantic interpretability of the identified patterns.
future_direction: Extending CAST to emerging transformer variants and next-generation architectures.
Integrating spectral analysis with existing probing and visualization techniques for semantic interpretability.
papers.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable success but remain largely black boxes with poorly understood internal mechanisms. To address this limitation, many researchers have proposed various interpretability methods including mechanistic analysis, probing classifiers, and activation visualization, each providing valuable insights from different perspectives. Building upon this rich landscape of complementary approaches, we introduce CAST (Compositional Analysis via Spectral Tracking), a probe-free framework that contributes a novel perspective by analyzing transformer layer functions through direct transformation matrix estimation and comprehensive spectral analysis. CAST offers complementary insights to existing methods by estimating the realized transformation matrices for each layer using Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse and applying spectral analysis with six interpretable metrics characterizing layer behavior. Our analysis reveals distinct behaviors between encoder-only and decoder-only models, with decoder models exhibiting compression-expansion cycles while encoder models maintain consistent high-rank processing. Kernel analysis further demonstrates functional relationship patterns between layers, with CKA similarity matrices clearly partitioning layers into three phases: feature extraction, compression, and specialization.

papers.title: Measuring the Mixing of Contextual Information in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How is contextual information mixed across the Transformer architecture, and how can this mixing be measured to provide faithful explanations for model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ALTI, an interpretability method that measures token-to-token interactions within each Transformer layer and aggregates them to provide input attribution scores, demonstrating more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: ALTI is a powerful interpretability method that quantifies the mixing of information in the Transformer, providing faithful input attributions and opening new possibilities for studying contextual information aggregation.
papers.key_findings:
ALTI outperforms gradient-based and other attribution methods in faithfulness metrics (comprehensiveness and sufficiency) across multiple models and datasets.
ALTI provides more robust interpretations across models with identical architecture but different random initializations, as measured by Jaccard similarity and Spearman correlation.
Using ℓ1 norm for measuring token contributions in ALTI is beneficial due to the anisotropic nature of Transformer representations and the presence of outlier dimensions.
The proposed layer-wise contribution measurement (based on distance to the output) significantly improves upon a previous norm-based approach.
Including the second layer normalization (from the feed-forward module) in the analysis has negligible impact on the faithfulness of the interpretations.
papers.limitation:
ALTI does not consider the classifier on top of the Transformer and therefore does not provide explanations for each of the output classes, unlike gradient-based methods.
Faithfulness is evaluated only via sufficiency and comprehensiveness metrics.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture aggregates input information through the self-attention mechanism, but there is no clear understanding of how this information is mixed across the entire model. Additionally, recent works have demonstrated that attention weights alone are not enough to describe the flow of information. In this paper, we consider the whole attention block --multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization-- and define a metric to measure token-to-token interactions within each layer. Then, we aggregate layer-wise interpretations to provide input attribution scores for model predictions. Experimentally, we show that our method, ALTI (Aggregation of Layer-wise Token-to-token Interactions), provides more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.

papers.title: Model learning with personalized interpretability estimation (ML-PIE)
papers.research_question: How can we synthesize models that are interpretable according to a specific user's subjective notion of interpretability by incorporating user feedback into the model synthesis process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ML-PIE, a human-in-the-loop active learning approach that synthesizes models with user-tailored interpretability by learning a personalized interpretability estimator from user feedback during the model synthesis process.
papers.conclusion: ML-PIE is a promising approach for synthesizing models with personalized interpretability, potentially advancing the field of explainable AI for high-stakes applications.
papers.key_findings:
ML-PIE can learn user-specific estimations of interpretability that can differ substantially across users.
The interpretability estimator in ML-PIE behaves sensibly, with low uncertainty and misprediction rates.
For more complex models, users tend to prefer models discovered by ML-PIE over those found using non-personalized interpretability indices (𝜙 and ℓ).
For simpler models, the choice of interpretability index does not significantly affect user preference.
The search performance of GP using the personalized estimator is not excessively harmed by the noise in the estimator.
papers.limitation:
The study did not involve actual domain experts and used a general set of model features for interpretability estimation.
The pace of user feedback may be too slow compared to the model synthesis process, which could harm the synthesis.
future_direction: Involve domain experts and add more specialized model features to the interpretability estimator.
Adapt ML-PIE to other model types (e.g., decision trees) and other model synthesis processes (e.g., reinforcement learning).
Study concurrency aspects, such as whether the model synthesis process should be halted based on the uncertainty of the interpretability estimator.
papers.abstract: High-stakes applications require AI-generated models to be interpretable. Current algorithms for the synthesis of potentially interpretable models rely on objectives or regularization terms that represent interpretability only coarsely (e.g., model size) and are not designed for a specific user. Yet, interpretability is intrinsically subjective. In this paper, we propose an approach for the synthesis of models that are tailored to the user by enabling the user to steer the model synthesis process according to her or his preferences. We use a bi-objective evolutionary algorithm to synthesize models with trade-offs between accuracy and a user-specific notion of interpretability. The latter is estimated by a neural network that is trained concurrently to the evolution using the feedback of the user, which is collected using uncertainty-based active learning. To maximize usability, the user is only asked to tell, given two models at the time, which one is less complex. With experiments on two real-world datasets involving 61 participants, we find that our approach is capable of learning estimations of interpretability that can be very different for different users. Moreover, the users tend to prefer models found using the proposed approach over models found using non-personalized interpretability indices.

papers.title: GlobEnc: Quantifying Global Token Attribution by Incorporating the Whole Encoder Layer in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we quantify global token attribution in Transformers by incorporating the whole encoder layer and aggregating across layers?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GlobEnc, a novel token attribution analysis method that incorporates all components in the Transformer encoder block (except the FFN) and aggregates attributions across layers using a modified rollout technique, yielding more faithful global token attributions.
papers.conclusion: GlobEnc provides faithful and meaningful global token attributions by incorporating the whole encoder layer and aggregating across layers, offering a valuable tool for interpreting Transformer-based models.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating vector norms yields higher correlation with gradient-based saliency scores than weight-based methods.
Residual connections play an essential role in token attribution and must be accurately modeled.
The two layer normalizations in the encoder counteract each other; incorporating both together is necessary for accurate analysis.
Aggregating attributions across layers via rollout is crucial for accurate whole-model attribution analysis.
GlobEnc significantly outperforms previous methods in correlation with gradient-based saliency scores across multiple tasks and models.
papers.limitation: The method omits the influence of the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) due to its non-linearity, which might affect the completeness of the attribution.
future_direction: Apply the global analysis method on various datasets and models to provide insights into model decisions and interpretability.
papers.abstract: Ali Modarressi, Mohsen Fayyaz, Yadollah Yaghoobzadeh, Mohammad Taher Pilehvar. Proceedings of the 2022 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies. 2022.

papers.title: Beyond Components: Singular Vector-Based Interpretability of Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: Can transformer components (attention heads and MLPs) be decomposed into orthogonal singular directions that reveal superposed and independent computations within a single head or MLP?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a directional interpretability perspective that decomposes transformer components into orthogonal singular directions, showing that multiple low-rank, interpretable computations coexist within single attention heads and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transformer computations are more distributed, structured, and compositional than previously assumed, opening new avenues for fine-grained mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of learned singular directions can faithfully preserve model behavior.
These directions align with meaningful subfunctions, e.g., in IOI, name mover heads encode multiple overlapping subfunctions along distinct singular directions.
Components identified as part of known circuits exhibit strong engagement along specific singular directions, indicating computations are embedded in compact subspaces.
Transformer computations are distributed, structured, and compositional, with overlapping subfunctions embedded within shared subspaces.
Singular directions can be used for controlled interventions, e.g., in gender pronoun resolution, scaling directions can modify predictions.
papers.limitation: Some directions remain challenging to interpret fully.
future_direction: Conduct targeted intervention experiments to validate causal contributions of discovered components.
Examine whether these mechanisms generalize to larger or more capable models (e.g., Phi, LLaMA).
Explore activation of these mechanisms in real-world settings.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit complex and distributed behavior, yet their internal computations remain poorly understood. Existing mechanistic interpretability methods typically treat attention heads and multilayer perceptron layers (MLPs) (the building blocks of a transformer architecture) as indivisible units, overlooking possibilities of functional substructure learned within them. In this work, we introduce a more fine-grained perspective that decomposes these components into orthogonal singular directions, revealing superposed and independent computations within a single head or MLP. We validate our perspective on widely used standard tasks like Indirect Object Identification (IOI), Gender Pronoun (GP), and Greater Than (GT), showing that previously identified canonical functional heads, such as the name mover, encode multiple overlapping subfunctions aligned with distinct singular directions. Nodes in a computational graph, that are previously identified as circuit elements show strong activation along specific low-rank directions, suggesting that meaningful computations reside in compact subspaces. While some directions remain challenging to interpret fully, our results highlight that transformer computations are more distributed, structured, and compositional than previously assumed. This perspective opens new avenues for fine-grained mechanistic interpretability and a deeper understanding of model internals.

papers.title: Naturalness of Attention: Revisiting Attention in Code Language Models
papers.research_question: How do the general trends across layers between attention weights and the scaled transformation norms compare, and how does the scaled transformation align with the syntactic structure of source code compared to attention weights?
papers.core_contribution: The scaled transformation norms of the input in attention mechanisms better capture syntactic structure in code compared to attention weights alone, revealing a cancellation effect between attention weights and transformation norms.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating scaled transformation norms provides new perspectives on what code properties are captured by attention, demonstrating that attention analysis should consider more than just attention weights for rigorous interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights and scaled transformation norms exhibit different trends across layers, with a cancellation effect observed between the two components.
Scaled transformation norms show higher alignment with syntactic properties of source code (as measured by AST agreement) than attention weights in most layers.
Special tokens like <s> and </s> receive high attention weights but contribute less in terms of scaled transformation norms, indicating attention weights alone may be misleading.
The alignment of scaled transformation norms with syntactic structure is evident from earlier layers compared to attention weights.
There are some layers where attention weights exhibit higher syntactic alignment than scaled transformation norms, indicating both factors are important for a complete understanding.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other models such as GraphCodeBERT and CodeT5.
Applying the methodology to other programming languages such as JavaScript and Go.
Investigating how specialized training objectives (e.g., in GraphCodeBERT, CodeT5) modify attention behaviors.
papers.abstract: Language models for code such as CodeBERT offer the capability to learn advanced source code representation, but their opacity poses barriers to understanding of captured properties. Recent attention analysis studies provide initial interpretability insights by focusing solely on attention weights rather than considering the wider context modeling of Transformers. This study aims to shed some light on the previously ignored factors of the attention mechanism beyond the attention weights. We conduct an initial empirical study analyzing both attention distributions and transformed representations in CodeBERT. Across two programming languages, Java and Python, we find that the scaled transformation norms of the input better capture syntactic structure compared to attention weights alone. Our analysis reveals characterization of how CodeBERT embeds syntactic code properties. The findings demonstrate the importance of incorporating factors beyond just attention weights for rigorously understanding neural code models. This lays the groundwork for developing more interpretable models and effective uses of attention mechanisms in program analysis.

papers.title: Birds have four legs?! NumerSense: Probing Numerical Commonsense Knowledge of Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: Does and to what extent do pre-trained language models capture numerical commonsense knowledge, and how robust is this knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a probing task and dataset (NumerSense) to evaluate numerical commonsense knowledge in pre-trained language models, finding that models perform poorly and are brittle to adversarial perturbations.
papers.conclusion: Powerful pre-trained models such as BERT and RoBERTa perform surprisingly poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge even after fine-tuning, and the introduced dataset provides a basis for future improvement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT and RoBERTa perform poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge without fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning with distant supervision improves performance but still far from human performance.
Models are brittle to adversarial examples (e.g., inserting adjectives).
Attention analysis shows that important words for numerical commonsense (subject/object) receive low attention weights.
Open-domain QA models also perform poorly on 'how-many' questions derived from NumerSense.
future_direction: Improving PTLMs' abilities to faithfully capture (numerical) commonsense.
Populating numerical facts in current commonsense knowledge bases.
Improving open-domain QA for 'how-many' questions.
Incorporating more structured inductive biases (e.g., dependencies and semantic roles) in pre-training.
Controlling bias in masked language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent works show that pre-trained language models (PTLMs), such as BERT, possess certain commonsense and factual knowledge. They suggest that it is promising to use PTLMs as "neural knowledge bases" via predicting masked words. Surprisingly, we find that this may not work for numerical commonsense knowledge (e.g., a bird usually has two legs). In this paper, we investigate whether and to what extent we can induce numerical commonsense knowledge from PTLMs as well as the robustness of this process. To study this, we introduce a novel probing task with a diagnostic dataset, NumerSense, containing 13.6k masked-word-prediction probes (10.5k for fine-tuning and 3.1k for testing). Our analysis reveals that: (1) BERT and its stronger variant RoBERTa perform poorly on the diagnostic dataset prior to any fine-tuning; (2) fine-tuning with distant supervision brings some improvement; (3) the best supervised model still performs poorly as compared to human performance (54.06% vs 96.3% in accuracy).

papers.title: Measuring the Interpretability and Explainability of Model Decisions of Five Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How interpretable and explainable are the decision-making processes of five leading LLMs, and what are their strengths and weaknesses in transparency and explanation accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive evaluation of the interpretability and explainability of five LLMs, revealing variability in their transparency and explanation accuracy, and proposes criteria for assessment and future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a foundational step towards demystifying the inner workings of LLMs, highlighting the importance of interpretability and explainability for trust and accountability, and suggests future research should focus on standardized assessment methodologies and enhancing model transparency.
papers.key_findings:
TripoSR and GemMoE-Beta-1 demonstrated superior transparency of reasoning.
Gemma-7b and Llama-2-7b excelled in the accuracy of their explanations.
Llama-2-7b and Gemma-7b demonstrated remarkable consistency across different contexts.
Mistral 7B and TripoSR showed outstanding adaptability to feedback.
There is a tension between increasing model complexity for performance gains and maintaining interpretability.
papers.limitation: The models show variability in interpretability and explainability across different contexts, and there is a trade-off between model complexity and interpretability.
future_direction: Developing standardized methodologies for assessing interpretability and explainability in LLMs.
Exploring innovative approaches to enhance model transparency.
Investigating the implications of interpretability and explainability on user trust and model adoption.
papers.abstract: This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of the interpretability and explainability of five leading Large Language Models (LLMs): TripoSR by Stability AI, Gemma-7b by Google, Mistral 7B by Mistral AI, Llama-2-7b by Meta, and GemMoE-Beta-1 by CrystalCare AI. Through a methodical evaluation encompassing both qualitative and quantitative benchmarks, we assess these models' capacity to make their decision-making processes understandable to humans. Our findings reveal significant variability in the models' ability to provide transparent reasoning and accurate, contextually relevant explanations across different contexts. Notably, TripoSR and GemMoE-Beta-1 demonstrated superior transparency, while Gemma-7b and Llama-2-7b excelled in the accuracy of their explanations. However, challenges in maintaining consistent interpretability and explainability across varying inputs and the need for enhanced adaptability to feedback highlight areas for future improvement. This research underscores the importance of interpretability and explainability in fostering trust and reliability in LLM applications, advocating for continued advancement in these areas to achieve more transparent, accountable, and user-centric AI systems. Directions for future research include the development of standardized evaluation methodologies and interdisciplinary approaches to enhance model transparency and user understanding.

papers.title: On the Impact of Knowledge Distillation for Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does knowledge distillation improve model interpretability in addition to model accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Knowledge distillation improves model interpretability by transferring class-similarity information from teacher to student, making activation maps more object-centric.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge distillation enhances both the accuracy and interpretability of models, and this improvement is consistent across different KD methods, datasets, and notions of interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
KD increases the number of concept detectors (interpretability) compared to training from scratch.
KD improves interpretability by transferring class-similarity information, while label smoothing reduces interpretability.
The interpretability of student models improves as the amount of class-similarity information they learn increases.
Various KD methods (vanilla KD, AT, FT, CRD, SSKD, self-KD) all improve model interpretability.
KD improves interpretability across different datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR, MNIST, SST) and different interpretability measures (concept detectors, five-band-scores, DiffROAR, loss gradients).
future_direction: Determine whether KD can yield other useful results (e.g., model robustness).
Explore whether additional metrics can be used to measure model interpretability.
papers.abstract: Several recent studies have elucidated why knowledge distillation (KD) improves model performance. However, few have researched the other advantages of KD in addition to its improving model performance. In this study, we have attempted to show that KD enhances the interpretability as well as the accuracy of models. We measured the number of concept detectors identified in network dissection for a quantitative comparison of model interpretability. We attributed the improvement in interpretability to the class-similarity information transferred from the teacher to student models. First, we confirmed the transfer of class-similarity information from the teacher to student model via logit distillation. Then, we analyzed how class-similarity information affects model interpretability in terms of its presence or absence and degree of similarity information. We conducted various quantitative and qualitative experiments and examined the results on different datasets, different KD methods, and according to different measures of interpretability. Our research showed that KD models by large models could be used more reliably in various fields.

papers.title: Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number
papers.research_question: How does BERT encode grammatical number, and does it actually use that encoding when solving the number agreement task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a usage-based probing setup to find functional encodings, and shows that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number for number agreement, with separate encodings for nouns and verbs, and identifies transfer layers.
papers.conclusion: The usage-based probing method allows tracking how grammatical number is encoded and transferred in BERT, showing that interventions impact behavior and extractability, revealing orthogonal encodings for nouns and verbs, and indirect transfer through intermediate tokens.
papers.key_findings:
BERT relies on a linear functional encoding of grammatical number to solve the number agreement task.
BERT uses separate encodings of grammatical number for nouns and verbs.
Number information is transferred from noun to verb between layers 3 and 8.
The transfer occurs indirectly through intermediate tokens, not directly via attention.
The encoding found by diagnostic probes is actually used by the model (functional).
papers.limitation:
The dataset may not be fully representative of the number agreement task.
Amnesic probing may remove more information than necessary.
papers.abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious-i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model's representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.

papers.title: Decomposing Query-Key Feature Interactions Using Contrastive Covariances
papers.research_question: Why does a model attend to a particular token? The paper investigates how to understand the inner structure of the query-key (QK) space in attention heads to explain attention patterns.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a contrastive covariance method to decompose the query-key (QK) space of attention heads into low-rank, interpretable components, enabling feature-based explanation of attention scores.
papers.conclusion: The contrastive covariance method provides a simple and effective way to decompose QK spaces into interpretable low-rank components, advancing our understanding of why models attend to specific tokens.
papers.key_findings:
The contrastive covariance method recovers the rank and subspaces of latent features in the QK space, as validated analytically and empirically in a toy model.
In large language models, the method identifies low-rank QK subspaces encoding categorical semantic features (e.g., fruits, animals) and binding features (e.g., order-ID, lexical-ID).
Causal interventions in the recovered subspaces demonstrate their role in attention, shifting attention when components are modified.
Attention logits can be attributed to the identified feature components, with a residual portion left unexplained, providing a decomposition of attention scores.
The method reveals feature splits and superposition in QK space, where features are compressed when dimensions are limited, highlighting limitations of interpretation.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on a human-defined notion of what constitutes a feature, via the design of positive and negative covariance conditions.
When the model compresses multiple features into fewer dimensions (superposition), the recovered components may be difficult to interpret.
The method requires knowing what features to look for beforehand, limiting unsupervised discovery.
Not all attention logits are explained by the identified features, indicating additional mechanisms may be at play.
future_direction: Unsupervised decomposition of QK spaces without human-defined features.
Detecting multi-dimensional features of varying ranks.
Interpreting components when multiple exhibit identical observable behaviors.
papers.abstract: Despite the central role of attention heads in Transformers, we lack tools to understand why a model attends to a particular token. To address this, we study the query-key (QK) space -- the bilinear joint embedding space between queries and keys. We present a contrastive covariance method to decompose the QK space into low-rank, human-interpretable components. It is when features in keys and queries align in these low-rank subspaces that high attention scores are produced. We first study our method both analytically and empirically in a simplified setting. We then apply our method to large language models to identify human-interpretable QK subspaces for categorical semantic features and binding features. Finally, we demonstrate how attention scores can be attributed to our identified features.

papers.title: Interpreting Deep Visual Representations via Network Dissection
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the interpretability of deep visual representations by aligning individual hidden units with visual semantic concepts, and what factors affect this interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Network Dissection, a method to quantify interpretability of deep visual representations by aligning individual units with visual concepts, and shows interpretability is axis-aligned and varies with architecture and training.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability is an important property of deep neural networks that provides new insights into their hierarchical structure.
papers.key_findings:
Deep visual representations are more interpretable than random bases of equivalent discriminative power.
Interpretability is an axis-aligned property that can be destroyed by rotating the representation.
Supervised training on large annotated datasets yields more object detectors than self-supervised training.
Batch normalization reduces interpretability while maintaining discriminative power.
Different network architectures and training conditions lead to varying levels of interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The method depends on the vocabulary of concepts in Broden; units detecting concepts not in Broden will not be counted.
The method measures alignment of individual units, so it may miss concepts represented by groups of units.
future_direction: Finding ways to capture the benefits of batch normalization without destroying interpretability.
Building more interpretable and explainable AI systems.
papers.abstract: The success of recent deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) depends on learning hidden representations that can summarize the important factors of variation behind the data. However, CNNs often criticized as being black boxes that lack interpretability, since they have millions of unexplained model parameters. In this work, we describe Network Dissection, a method that interprets networks by providing labels for the units of their deep visual representations. The proposed method quantifies the interpretability of CNN representations by evaluating the alignment between individual hidden units and a set of visual semantic concepts. By identifying the best alignments, units are given human interpretable labels across a range of objects, parts, scenes, textures, materials, and colors. The method reveals that deep representations are more transparent and interpretable than expected: we find that representations are significantly more interpretable than they would be under a random equivalently powerful basis. We apply the method to interpret and compare the latent representations of various network architectures trained to solve different supervised and self-supervised training tasks. We then examine factors affecting the network interpretability such as the number of the training iterations, regularizations, different initializations, and the network depth and width. Finally we show that the interpreted units can be used to provide explicit explanations of a prediction given by a CNN for an image. Our results highlight that interpretability is an important property of deep neural networks that provides new insights into their hierarchical structure.

papers.title: Decompose the model: Mechanistic interpretability in image models with Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG)
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be achieved in image models by systematically tracing the pathway from input to output across an entire dataset, moving beyond class-specific explanations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel approach for mechanistic interpretability in image models, using Pointwise Feature Vectors (PFVs) and Effective Receptive Fields (ERFs) to decompose model embeddings into interpretable Concept Vectors, and a new Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG) method to trace their causal contributions across layers for a dataset-wide analysis.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a novel approach for extracting and attributing concepts within image models, enabling a comprehensive layer-wise analysis that advances mechanistic interpretability by moving from class-specific to dataset-wide explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The method can extract and attribute 'shared concepts' that are common across similar classes, unlike class-specific explanation methods.
The proposed concept extraction method using bisecting k-means clustering outperforms other methods (like Sparse AutoEncoder and dictionary learning) in fidelity metrics (C-Deletion and C-Insertion) across most layers.
The Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG) method effectively quantifies the causal relationships between concept vectors across different layers, validated by inter-layer deletion/insertion experiments.
The approach provides a holistic, dataset-wide understanding of model behavior, tracing how concepts are constructed and aggregated from lower to higher layers.
future_direction: Extending the method to other deep learning architectures, such as Transformer models.
More thoroughly investigating the implications of analyzing entire datasets rather than focusing solely on class-specific explanations.
papers.abstract: In the field of eXplainable AI (XAI) in language models, the progression from local explanations of individual decisions to global explanations with high-level concepts has laid the groundwork for mechanistic interpretability, which aims to decode the exact operations. However, this paradigm has not been adequately explored in image models, where existing methods have primarily focused on class-specific interpretations. This paper introduces a novel approach to systematically trace the entire pathway from input through all intermediate layers to the final output within the whole dataset. We utilize Pointwise Feature Vectors (PFVs) and Effective Receptive Fields (ERFs) to decompose model embeddings into interpretable Concept Vectors. Then, we calculate the relevance between concept vectors with our Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG), enabling a comprehensive, dataset-wide analysis of model behavior. We validate our method of concept extraction and concept attribution in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. Our approach advances the understanding of semantic significance within image models, offering a holistic view of their operational mechanics.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition.
