papers.research_question: How can we explain the predictions of chemical language models by attributing importance to individual atoms in the input molecular string?
papers.core_contribution: We propose an explainable AI technique for chemical language models that attributes the importance of individual atoms to the model's predictions by backpropagating relevance through attention scores and gradients, and visualize the importance on the molecular structure.
papers.conclusion: We propose an attribution technique for Transformers operating on molecular string representations, which provides interpretable predictions and allows inspection of the model's learned features for solubility prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves competitive predictive performance on aqueous and organic solvent solubility prediction tasks.
The visualizations highlight atoms that are important for solubility, which can be validated by chemists.
The model sometimes attributes high relevance to the carbon backbone, which may be due to the pretraining procedure.
The method is applicable to self-attention Transformers and can be extended to other architectures.
papers.limitation:
The method only visualizes atom tokens and does not handle non-atom tokens (e.g., bonds, brackets) in the SMILES string.
The model does not enforce invariance to different SMILES representations of the same molecule.
future_direction: Extend the visualization to non-atom tokens in the SMILES string.
Enforce SMILES invariance in the model through contrastive training.
Apply the explainability technique to other Transformer architectures, such as generative models.
papers.abstract: Explainability techniques are crucial in gaining insights into the reasons behind the predictions of deep learning models, which have not yet been applied to chemical language models. We propose an explainable AI technique that attributes the importance of individual atoms towards the predictions made by these models. Our method backpropagates the relevance information towards the chemical input string and visualizes the importance of individual atoms. We focus on self-attention Transformers operating on molecular string representations and leverage a pretrained encoder for finetuning. We showcase the method by predicting and visualizing solubility in water and organic solvents. We achieve competitive model performance while obtaining interpretable predictions, which we use to inspect the pretrained model.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Automated Interpretability Metrics Do Not Distinguish Trained and Random Transformers
papers.research_question: Do commonly used SAE quality metrics and automatic explanation pipelines distinguish trained transformers from randomly initialized ones?
papers.core_contribution: Common SAE metrics (e.g., auto-interpretability scores) do not reliably distinguish between trained and randomly initialized transformers, indicating these metrics are insufficient for validating interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: High aggregate auto-interpretability scores alone do not guarantee that learned, computationally relevant features have been recovered; the paper recommends routine randomized baselines and targeted measures of feature 'abstractness'.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on randomly initialized transformers produce auto-interpretability scores and reconstruction metrics similar to those from trained models.
Standard SAE quality metrics (explained variance, cosine similarity, L1 norm) show similar trends across trained and randomized variants.
Token distribution entropy reveals that features from randomized models remain simple and token-specific, unlike features from trained models which become more abstract across layers.
The area under the ROC curve (AUROC) for auto-interpretability tasks does not meaningfully discriminate between trained and randomized transformers in many settings.
Randomly initialized neural networks can preserve or amplify superposition present in input data, which may explain the similar SAE performance.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to Pythia models and the RedPajama dataset; results may vary with other architectures or data.
future_direction: Develop better metrics to distinguish between artifacts and genuinely learned computations in interpretability methods.
Investigate why randomly initialized transformers produce SAE metrics similar to trained ones, e.g., whether they preserve or amplify superposition.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used to extract sparse, interpretable latents from transformer activations. We test whether commonly used SAE quality metrics and automatic explanation pipelines can distinguish trained transformers from randomly initialized ones (e.g., where parameters are sampled i.i.d. from a Gaussian). Over a wide range of Pythia model sizes and multiple randomization schemes, we find that, in many settings, SAEs trained on randomly initialized transformers produce auto-interpretability scores and reconstruction metrics that are similar to those from trained models. These results show that high aggregate auto-interpretability scores do not, by themselves, guarantee that learned, computationally relevant features have been recovered. We therefore recommend treating common SAE metrics as useful but insufficient proxies for mechanistic interpretability and argue for routine randomized baselines and targeted measures of feature 'abstractness'.

papers.title: Multi-Head Attention: Collaborate Instead of Concatenate
papers.research_question: How redundant are the key/query projections in multi-head attention, and can we design a more parameter-efficient multi-head attention mechanism by sharing these projections?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes collaborative multi-head attention, which shares key/query projections across heads, reducing parameters without performance loss and enabling post-hoc compression of pre-trained models.
papers.conclusion: Collaborative multi-head attention is a more efficient alternative to concatenation-based multi-head attention, reducing redundancy and enabling parameter reduction without performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Heads in standard multi-head attention learn redundant key/query projections, as shown by PCA.
Collaborative attention can reduce the key/query dimension by 4x without performance drop in NMT and vision tasks.
Pre-trained models can be re-parametrized into collaborative attention via tensor decomposition, allowing compression without retraining.
Collaborative attention consistently improves over concatenation-based attention with the same number of parameters.
The method is effective across modalities (text and image) and various transformer architectures (BERT, DistilBERT, ALBERT, DeiT).
papers.limitation: ALBERT suffers more from compression, possibly because it already shares parameters across layers, which may limit the redundancy that can be exploited.
papers.abstract: Attention layers are widely used in natural language processing (NLP) and are beginning to influence computer vision architectures. Training very large transformer models allowed significant improvement in both fields, but once trained, these networks show symptoms of over-parameterization. For instance, it is known that many attention heads can be pruned without impacting accuracy. This work aims to enhance current understanding on how multiple heads interact. Motivated by the observation that attention heads learn redundant key/query projections, we propose a collaborative multi-head attention layer that enables heads to learn shared projections. Our scheme decreases the number of parameters in an attention layer and can be used as a drop-in replacement in any transformer architecture. Our experiments confirm that sharing key/query dimensions can be exploited in language understanding, machine translation and vision. We also show that it is possible to re-parametrize a pre-trained multi-head attention layer into our collaborative attention layer. Collaborative multi-head attention reduces the size of the key and query projections by 4 for same accuracy and speed. Our code is public.

papers.title: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.research_question: Does injecting linguistic structure into language models lead to better alignment with brain recordings?
papers.core_contribution: Injecting linguistic structure bias into language models via guided attention during fine-tuning can improve alignment with brain recordings, particularly for word-level fMRI data.
papers.conclusion: Injecting linguistic structure bias through guided attention can improve brain decoding performance, with clearer benefits for finer-grained (word-level) analyses, and highlights the importance of controlling for domain effects.
papers.key_findings:
For the word-level Wehbe2014 fMRI dataset, guided attention models significantly outperform pretrained and domain-finetuned baselines in brain decoding.
For the sentence-level Pereira2018 dataset, improvements are more modest, with UD and DM guided attention models showing some improvement over the pretrained baseline.
Domain of the fine-tuning data is an important confound affecting brain alignment; simply fine-tuning on a different domain can reduce alignment.
Guided attention models perform better on subject-verb agreement syntactic probing tasks, with performance ranking corresponding to brain decoding scores.
Guided attention improves performance on a semantic tagging task for most semantic categories, especially discourse and temporal relations.
papers.limitation:
The fMRI data was recorded during passive reading without a specific task, which may limit the ability to uncover fine-grained patterns of linguistic structure.
Potential confounds such as domain, corpus size, and dependency length differences between the linguistic formalisms are not fully controlled for due to the lack of a common annotated corpus.
future_direction: Investigating brain alignment using continuous, naturalistic listening fMRI datasets.
Using a common annotated corpus for all formalisms to properly control for confounds like domain and corpus size.
papers.abstract: Neuroscientists evaluate deep neural networks for natural language processing as possible candidate models for how language is processed in the brain. These models are often trained without explicit linguistic supervision, but have been shown to learn some linguistic structure in the absence of such supervision (Manning et al., 2020), potentially questioning the relevance of symbolic linguistic theories in modeling such cognitive processes (Warstadt and Bowman, 2020). We evaluate across two fMRI datasets whether language models align better with brain recordings, if their attention is biased by annotations from syntactic or semantic formalisms. Using structure from dependency or minimal recursion semantic annotations, we find alignments improve significantly for one of the datasets. For another dataset, we see more mixed results. We present an extensive analysis of these results. Our proposed approach enables the evaluation of more targeted hypotheses about the composition of meaning in the brain, expanding the range of possible scientific inferences a neuroscientist could make, and opens up new opportunities for cross-pollination between computational neuroscience and linguistics.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: Ecco: An Open Source Library for the Explainability of Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the level of syntactic information in BERT's FFNN representations compared to hidden states, and how does syntactic information evolve across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Ecco, an open-source library for explainability of Transformer language models, and uses it to find that syntactic information in BERT's FFNN representations is comparable to hidden states, and that hidden states build up syntactic information even when intermediate FFNNs show diminished levels.
papers.conclusion: Ecco is a tool that aids in debugging, explaining, and building intuitions about Transformer language models, and it is open-source for community contribution.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic information can be retrieved from BERT's FFNN representations at levels comparable to hidden state representations.
The model builds up syntactic information in its hidden states even when intermediate FFNNs indicate diminished levels of syntactic information.
Ecco provides tools for input saliency (gradient-based feature attribution), hidden state evolution analysis, and neuron activation analysis via dimensionality reduction and probing.
The library supports multiple explainability methods (e.g., CCA, NMF, probing) and models (GPT2, BERT, RoBERTa).
Ecco enables interactive exploration of model internals within Jupyter notebooks.
papers.limitation:
Ecco's input saliency feature is currently only supported for GPT2-based models, while neuron activation collection and dimensionality reduction are supported for GPT2, BERT, and RoBERTa.
Visualization is a starting point for building testable and falsifiable hypotheses of model interpretability, not a definitive explanation.
future_direction: Support for more models and explainability methods is under development and open for community contribution.
Future work can examine if the divergence in PoS information between FFNN and hidden states points towards layers storing different subsets of PoS information which the model assembles across layers.
papers.abstract: J Alammar. Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations. 2021.

papers.title: On Hierarchical Encoding and Reasoning in Deep Transformer-based Generative Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internalize hierarchical structures from data, what is the relationship between this internalization and behaviors like generalization versus memorization, and how can insights into hierarchical reasoning guide the development of more unified, robust, and interpretable multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis investigates how Transformer models learn and represent hierarchical structures, develops methods to probe these structures and mitigate harmful memorization, introduces the PSViT model for hierarchical video prediction, and demonstrates a unified next-frame prediction framework for multimodal tasks.
papers.conclusion: The capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional Transformer models (e.g., BERT) concentrate hierarchical linguistic information near the top layers, while autoregressive/permutation-masked models (e.g., GPT-2, XLNet, Reformer) distribute it more evenly.
Verbatim memorization during fine-tuning is often preceded by a spike in n-gram overlap, which can be used for early-stopping or regularization to reduce leakage by up to 90%.
The PSViT model, designed with hierarchical priors, outperforms latent-space baselines on physical simulation benchmarks, extending accurate prediction horizons by up to 50%.
Abstract physical parameters governing video dynamics are most linearly recoverable from the middle layers of PSViT, mirroring the mid-layer abstraction peak for linguistic hierarchy.
Diverse tasks across text, image, audio, and video can be reformulated into a unified next-frame prediction task, enabling a single PSViT-based model to achieve competitive performance without modality-specific encoders.
papers.limitation:
Probing tasks relied primarily on English datasets (SST, PTB), limiting linguistic diversity.
Memorization experiments used datasets of up to 5,000 samples and greedy decoding; different scales or decoding strategies may alter dynamics.
PSViT was evaluated at 128x128 resolution on deterministic simulations; generalizability to complex real-world video is untested.
The multimodal model was trained separately per task; joint multitask training might better foster shared representations.
future_direction: Extend ancestor probing to morphologically rich languages, different syntactic formalisms, and broader discourse structures.
Scale the n-gram-aware loss regularizer to operate efficiently on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Test PSViT on larger-scale, stochastic, real-world video and integrate differentiable renderers for more direct interpretability.
Explore joint multitask training on a diverse corpus of reformulated multimodal data and richer encodings within the visual canvas.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative Transformer-based foundation models have driven remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, yet their internal mechanisms for representing complex hierarchical structures remain largely unknown, posing significant challenges for interpretability, safety, and robust generalisation. This thesis aims to progress on these issues by systematically investigating how such models internalise hierarchical structures, the relationship between this learning and behaviours like generalisation versus memorisation, and how hierarchical principles can inform the development of safer, more accurate, generative models. To this end, we first introduce novel probing techniques to map the layer-wise emergence of linguistic hierarchies in language models and extend this analysis to the visual domain by developing PSViT: a pixel-space Transformer with hierarchical decompositions of video image patches, shown to learn and generalise hierarchical physical dynamics from raw video data. We investigate memorisation during fine-tuning, establishing an n-gram based early warning signal for verbatim leakage and proposing scalable defences that promote structural generalisation over verbatim memorisation. Building on these insights, we further demonstrate that a unified next-frame prediction framework enables a single model to process text, images, audio, and video without modality-specific encoders, thereby learning shared hierarchical patterns across these diverse inputs. Collectively, our findings underscore that the capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and that a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Capturing Polysemanticity with PRISM: A Multi-Concept Feature Description Framework
papers.research_question: How can we capture polysemanticity (multiple concepts per feature) in large language models to improve automated feature description methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PRISM, a framework for generating multi-concept feature descriptions that captures polysemanticity in LLMs, outperforming single-concept methods in description quality and faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: PRISM provides a more nuanced and accurate understanding of feature polysemanticity in LLMs, advancing automated interpretability by moving beyond single-concept descriptions.
papers.key_findings:
PRISM (max) achieves higher AUROC and MAD scores than existing feature description methods across multiple models and feature types.
PRISM reveals that individual features often encode a diverse set of concepts, demonstrating polysemanticity.
The degree of polysemanticity varies across model layers and architectures, with no consistent trend with depth.
Neuron-based features (MLP) are generally more interpretable than SAE-based features from the residual stream.
The framework is robust to variations in clustering parameters and the choice of language model for description generation.
papers.limitation: Relies on the quality of clustering and the language model used for description generation, which may produce unfaithful explanations.
future_direction: Extending PRISM to other modalities, such as vision or multimodal models.
Investigating the relationship between polysemanticity and model performance.
papers.abstract: Automated interpretability research aims to identify concepts encoded in neural network features to enhance human understanding of model behavior. Within the context of large language models (LLMs) for natural language processing (NLP), current automated neuron-level feature description methods face two key challenges: limited robustness and the assumption that each neuron encodes a single concept (monosemanticity), despite increasing evidence of polysemanticity. This assumption restricts the expressiveness of feature descriptions and limits their ability to capture the full range of behaviors encoded in model internals. To address this, we introduce Polysemantic FeatuRe Identification and Scoring Method (PRISM), a novel framework specifically designed to capture the complexity of features in LLMs. Unlike approaches that assign a single description per neuron, common in many automated interpretability methods in NLP, PRISM produces more nuanced descriptions that account for both monosemantic and polysemantic behavior. We apply PRISM to LLMs and, through extensive benchmarking against existing methods, demonstrate that our approach produces more accurate and faithful feature descriptions, improving both overall description quality (via a description score) and the ability to capture distinct concepts when polysemanticity is present (via a polysemanticity score).

papers.title: SocioProbe: What, When, and Where Language Models Learn about Sociodemographics
papers.research_question: What, when, and where do language models learn about sociodemographics? Specifically, to what extent do they encode such knowledge, how much pre-training data is needed, where in the model is it located, does it differ in multilingual models, and what is the effect of supplementary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SocioProbe, a method to probe sociodemographic knowledge in PLMs, and finds that such knowledge is encoded but is more diffuse than lower-level linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: We find that sociodemographic knowledge is located in PLMs, but much more diffuse than lower-level aspects. We hope that our findings will fuel further research towards human-like language understanding.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs encode sociodemographic knowledge, but the extent varies across models and textual domains.
Sociodemographic knowledge requires large amounts of pre-training data and learning curves do not flatten.
Sociodemographic knowledge is less localized in model layers compared to syntactic knowledge (e.g., CoLA).
In multilingual models, the localization of sociodemographic knowledge is similar to monolingual models.
Supplementary training on intermediate tasks (STILTs) can overwrite sociodemographic knowledge in the higher layers.
papers.limitation:
Predictive methods can result in potentially harmful applications (dual use).
Gender is modeled as a binary variable, not reflecting the full spectrum of identities.
Models are limited to single-GPU, general-purpose pre-trained models; results may differ for larger or domain-specific models.
future_direction: Extend analysis to languages other than English
Explore models with different architectures and pre-training objectives
Investigate sociodemographic knowledge in larger and domain-specific models
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have outperformed other NLP models on a wide range of tasks. Opting for a more thorough understanding of their capabilities and inner workings, researchers have established the extend to which they capture lower-level knowledge like grammaticality, and mid-level semantic knowledge like factual understanding. However, there is still little understanding of their knowledge of higher-level aspects of language. In particular, despite the importance of sociodemographic aspects in shaping our language, the questions of whether, where, and how PLMs encode these aspects, e.g., gender or age, is still unexplored. We address this research gap by probing the sociodemographic knowledge of different single-GPU PLMs on multiple English data sets via traditional classifier probing and information-theoretic minimum description length probing. Our results show that PLMs do encode these sociodemographics, and that this knowledge is sometimes spread across the layers of some of the tested PLMs. We further conduct a multilingual analysis and investigate the effect of supplementary training to further explore to what extent, where, and with what amount of pre-training data the knowledge is encoded. Our overall results indicate that sociodemographic knowledge is still a major challenge for NLP. PLMs require large amounts of pre-training data to acquire the knowledge and models that excel in general language understanding do not seem to own more knowledge about these aspects.

papers.title: Stream: Scaling up Mechanistic Interpretability to Long Context in LLMs via Sparse Attention
papers.research_question: How to scale mechanistic interpretability techniques to long contexts in LLMs, given the quadratic scaling of attention? Specifically, how to efficiently analyze attention patterns in long contexts with near-linear time and memory?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SPARSETRACING and STREAM, a scalable framework and algorithm for mechanistic interpretability in long-context LLMs, achieving near-linear time and linear memory complexity by leveraging hierarchical sparse attention pruning.
papers.conclusion: SPARSETRACING and STREAM provide scalable tools for mechanistic interpretability in long-context LLMs, enabling experiments previously infeasible due to quadratic complexity, and democratizing long-context interpretability on consumer hardware.
papers.key_findings:
STREAM prunes 97-99% of attention links in chain-of-thought reasoning traces while preserving model output, identifying thought anchors.
On the RULER benchmark, STREAM preserves critical retrieval paths while discarding 90-96% of interactions, exposing layer-wise routes from needle to output.
STREAM enables interpretability of million-token contexts on consumer GPUs, reducing resource costs by up to four orders of magnitude.
Needle retrieval is more robust for needles earlier in the context, and pruning weakens retrieval towards the end of longer contexts.
STREAM's sparse masks highlight the same key structures as dense patterns but with linear scaling, making long-context interpretability feasible.
papers.limitation:
STREAM focuses only on the attention mechanism and does not account for residual connections and MLP layers.
The method's success is defined by a proxy metric (two consecutive correct tokens), which may not fully capture model performance or complete causal paths.
The current implementation is not optimized for specific hardware and runs slower than desired.
The pruning algorithm is more aggressive towards the bottom of the attention pattern, which could be resolved by implementing variable sparsity constant k.
Future work introducing a novel discovery made by STREAM would truly validate the method's applicability.
future_direction: Incorporate MLP layers and residual stream analysis into the SPARSETRACING framework.
Establish theoretical guarantees about what types of circuits and information pathways are preserved under different sparsity levels.
Use STREAM to study long context phenomena like information over-squashing, over-smoothing, and under-reaching.
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) scale to million-token contexts, traditional Mechanistic Interpretability techniques for analyzing attention scale quadratically with context length, demanding terabytes of memory beyond 100,000 tokens. We introduce Sparse Tracing, a novel technique that leverages dynamic sparse attention to efficiently analyze long context attention patterns. We present Stream, a compilable hierarchical pruning algorithm that estimates per-head sparse attention masks in near-linear time $O(T \log T)$ and linear space $O(T)$, enabling one-pass interpretability at scale. Stream performs a binary-search-style refinement to retain only the top-$k$ key blocks per query while preserving the model's next-token behavior. We apply Stream to long chain-of-thought reasoning traces and identify thought anchors while pruning 97-99\% of token interactions. On the RULER benchmark, Stream preserves critical retrieval paths while discarding 90-96\% of interactions and exposes layer-wise routes from the needle to output. Our method offers a practical drop-in tool for analyzing attention patterns and tracing information flow without terabytes of caches. By making long context interpretability feasible on consumer GPUs, Sparse Tracing helps democratize chain-of-thought monitoring. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/stream-03B8/.

papers.title: Beyond Activation Patterns: A Weight-Based Out-of-Context Explanation of Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we interpret Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features from a weight-based, out-of-context perspective to understand their computational roles, beyond activation patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a weight-based, out-of-context interpretation framework for SAE features that reveals their computational roles in output prediction and attention mechanisms, complementing activation-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Weight-based, out-of-context analysis provides the missing half of SAE feature interpretability, revealing computational roles and depth-dependent functional specialization that activation patterns alone cannot capture.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 1/4 of SAE features directly predict output tokens when analyzed through their decoder-unembedding interactions.
Semantic features exhibit a U-shaped distribution across depth in Gemma models (high in early and late layers) and a monotonic distribution in Llama models, revealing architectural differences in functional specialization.
Features actively participate in attention mechanisms, with pre- and post-softmax analysis showing depth-dependent structure and distinct profiles for semantic vs. non-semantic populations.
Weight-based analysis uncovers that early-layer features in Llama specialize for input token recognition (encoder-embedding alignment) while late-layer features specialize for output prediction (decoder-unembedding alignment).
The out-of-context framework provides a complementary, causal perspective on feature function that activation-based methods miss.
papers.limitation:
The out-of-context framework is strict and simulates attention competition across the entire SAE dictionary, which may not reflect the contextual sparsity of actual forward passes and could underestimate feature importance.
The analysis focuses on intra-layer attention (features in layer L interacting with QK circuits in layer L+1) and may miss features specialized for longer-range, inter-layer interactions.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful technique for decomposing language model representations into interpretable features. Current interpretation methods infer feature semantics from activation patterns, but overlook that features are trained to reconstruct activations that serve computational roles in the forward pass. We introduce a novel weight-based interpretation framework that measures functional effects through direct weight interactions, requiring no activation data. Through three experiments on Gemma-2 and Llama-3.1 models, we demonstrate that (1) 1/4 of features directly predict output tokens, (2) features actively participate in attention mechanisms with depth-dependent structure, and (3) semantic and non-semantic feature populations exhibit distinct distribution profiles in attention circuits. Our analysis provides the missing out-of-context half of SAE feature interpretability.

papers.title: Exploration and adaptation of large language models for specialized domains
papers.research_question: Can large language models overcome challenges in specialized domains, and how can they be effectively adapted to domain-specific requirements?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation provides insights into the inner workings of LLMs and proposes adaptation methods that demonstrate LLMs can be effectively used in specialized domains, particularly clinical NLP.
papers.conclusion: The work provides new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models and multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.
papers.key_findings:
Layers of Transformer-based LLMs encode different dimensions of input text, with contextual representations and general language knowledge being beneficial for complex tasks.
Pre-trained language models outperform traditional approaches on clinical tasks.
Integration of domain-specific resources (like ICD hierarchy) improves model generalization.
Behavioral testing framework can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts.
Prototypical networks can provide interpretable diagnosis predictions.
papers.limitation: There is no ground truth in clinical data
future_direction: Integration of multimodal and multilingual data
Efficient methods for large language models
papers.abstract: Large language models have transformed the field of natural language processing (NLP). Their improved performance on various NLP benchmarks makes them a promising tool—also for the application in specialized domains. Such domains are characterized by highly trained professionals with particular domain expertise. Since these experts are rare, improving the efficiency of their work with automated systems is especially desirable. However, domain-specific text resources hold various challenges for NLP systems. These challenges include distinct language, noisy and scarce data, and a high level of variation. Further, specialized domains present an increased need for transparent systems since they are often applied in high stakes settings. In this dissertation, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can overcome some of these challenges and propose methods to effectively adapt them to domain-specific requirements. We first investigate the inner workings and abilities of LLMs and show how they can fill the gaps that are present in previous NLP algorithms for specialized domains. To this end, we explore the sources of errors produced by earlier systems to identify which of them can be addressed by using LLMs. Following this, we take a closer look at how information is processed within Transformer-based LLMs to better understand their capabilities. We find that their layers encode different dimensions of the input text. Here, the contextual vector representation, and the general language knowledge learned during pre-training are especially beneficial for solving complex and multi-step tasks common in specialized domains. Following this exploration, we propose solutions for further adapting LLMs to the requirements of domain-specific tasks. We focus on the clinical domain, which incorporates many typical challenges found in specialized domains. We show how to improve generalization by integrating different domain-specific resources into our models. We further analyze the behavior of the produced models and propose a behavioral testing framework that can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts. Finally, we present an approach for incorporating the benefits of LLMs while fulfilling requirements such as interpretability and modularity. The presented solutions show improvements in performance on benchmark datasets and in manually conducted analyses with medical professionals. Our work provides both new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models as well as multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.

papers.title: Learning to Disentangle Latent Reasoning Rules with Language VAEs: A Systematic Study
papers.research_question: How can reasoning rules be explicitly encoded within the latent space of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a complete pipeline for learning reasoning rules within Transformer-based language VAEs, encompassing three rule-based reasoning tasks, a supporting theoretical framework based on Neural Tangent Kernel theory, and a practical end-to-end architecture.
papers.conclusion: This work serves as a foundational step in exploring rule-based representation learning under the language VAE architecture for NLI tasks, demonstrating that reasoning rules can be disentangled in the encoder's parametric space and that injecting latent reasoning representations into the decoder's query improves performance.
papers.key_findings:
Under explicit signal supervision, reasoning rules can be disentangled within the encoder’s parametric space, resulting in distinct clustering of rules in the output feature space.
Injecting reasoning information into the Query of the attention mechanism enables the model to more effectively retrieve the stored Value from memory based on Key, offering a simple method for integrating prior knowledge into decoder-only language models.
FFN layers are better than attention layers at preserving the separation of reasoning rules in the model’s parameters.
Increasing the number of training samples per operation beyond a threshold (around 2000) leads to a decline in accuracy, indicating an information bottleneck where models rely on memorization rather than rule-based reasoning.
Integrating BM25-based sample selection during training yields enhanced performance, indicating the effectiveness of relevance-guided sampling.
papers.limitation: This study does not aim to explore rule composition or generalisation.
future_direction: Investigation of diffusion-based language models, such as Mmada, to improve flexibility for constraining the decoding process.
papers.abstract: Incorporating explicit reasoning rules within the latent space of language models (LMs) offers a promising pathway to enhance generalisation, interpretability, and controllability. While current Transformer-based language models have shown strong performance on Natural Language Inference (NLI) tasks, they often rely on memorisation rather than rule-based inference. This work investigates how reasoning rules can be explicitly embedded and memorised within the LMs through Language Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). We propose a complete pipeline for learning reasoning rules within Transformer-based language VAEs. This pipeline encompasses three rule-based reasoning tasks, a supporting theoretical framework, and a practical end-to-end architecture. The experiment illustrates the following findings: Disentangled reasoning: Under explicit signal supervision, reasoning rules - viewed as functional mappings - can be disentangled within the encoder's parametric space. This separation results in distinct clustering of rules in the output feature space. Prior knowledge injection: injecting reasoning information into the Query enables the model to more effectively retrieve the stored value Value from memory based on Key. This approach offers a simple method for integrating prior knowledge into decoder-only language models. Performance bottleneck: In mathematical reasoning tasks using Qwen2.5(0.5B), increasing sample count doesn't improve performance beyond a point. Moreover, ffn layers are better than attention layers at preserving the separation of reasoning rules in the model's parameters.

papers.title: BERT Learns (and Teaches) Chemistry
papers.research_question: Can attention mechanisms in BERT be used to identify important molecular substructures (functional groups) from SMILES string representations and apply these learned representations to chemical property prediction tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that BERT's attention mechanisms can identify chemically relevant functional groups from SMILES strings without domain heuristics, and that these learned representations can be applied to downstream chemical property prediction tasks.
papers.conclusion: Attention visualization in BERT provides a data-driven method to identify functional groups and important molecular substructures from SMILES strings, offering a potentially useful tool for computational chemistry despite not achieving state-of-the-art performance on downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's attention heads, trained only on SMILES strings, learn to attend to atoms that correspond to known active reaction sites (functional groups) in molecules, even without explicit reaction data.
When fine-tuned on chemical property regression tasks (e.g., solubility), specific attention heads in BERT focus on relevant substructures (e.g., carbon chains for solubility).
Using BERT embeddings as features for graph models (GCN, GAT) on toxicity prediction tasks yields competitive but not state-of-the-art performance compared to canonical atom featurization.
Attention visualization of BERT trained on chemical data can serve as a tool for chemistry practitioners to quickly identify important substructures related to various chemical properties.
papers.limitation:
BERT embeddings did not improve upon the state of the art when used as features for graph models on toxicity prediction; the learned information appears to be a subset of that captured by canonical atom featurization.
Some molecules in the Tox21 dataset contain atoms not present in BERT's vocabulary, which may detract from performance.
Attention heads after fine-tuning on most chemical property tasks (QED, SAS) showed little change from pretraining, except for the solubility task, suggesting the fine-tuning may find a local optimum close to pretraining weights.
future_direction: Using a larger dataset of 96 million molecules from PubMed to train BERT, given that language models thrive with abundant data.
Designing a loss function that penalizes distances between embeddings of different SMILES strings representing the same molecule to force BERT to learn the inherent graphical meaning.
Further investigating the approach of analyzing chemical property-bearing molecular substructures via fine-tuning to make it a more useful tool for chemists.
papers.abstract: Modern computational organic chemistry is becoming increasingly data-driven. There remain a large number of important unsolved problems in this area such as product prediction given reactants, drug discovery, and metric-optimized molecule synthesis, but efforts to solve these problems using machine learning have also increased in recent years. In this work, we propose the use of attention to study functional groups and other property-impacting molecular substructures from a data-driven perspective, using a transformer-based model (BERT) on datasets of string representations of molecules and analyzing the behavior of its attention heads. We then apply the representations of functional groups and atoms learned by the model to tackle problems of toxicity, solubility, drug-likeness, and synthesis accessibility on smaller datasets using the learned representations as features for graph convolution and attention models on the graph structure of molecules, as well as fine-tuning of BERT. Finally, we propose the use of attention visualization as a helpful tool for chemistry practitioners and students to quickly identify important substructures in various chemical properties.

papers.title: XAI-Driven Deep Learning for Protein Sequence Functional Group Classification
papers.research_question: How do different deep learning architectures perform on protein functional group classification, and how can explainable AI techniques reveal biologically meaningful sequence motifs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a comparative deep learning framework for protein functional group classification, demonstrating that CNNs achieve the highest accuracy, and uses explainable AI techniques (Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients) to identify biologically relevant sequence motifs.
papers.conclusion: Deep learning architectures, particularly CNNs, can achieve high predictive accuracy for protein functional group classification, and explainable AI techniques successfully uncover biologically meaningful sequence motifs that align with known catalytic mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN model achieved the highest validation accuracy (91.8%) for protein functional group classification.
Explainable AI techniques revealed motifs enriched in histidine, aspartate, glutamate, and lysine, residues commonly associated with catalytic and metal-binding sites in enzymes.
Different architectures focus on motifs differently: CNNs emphasize localized motifs, BiLSTMs distribute relevance across broader regions, and attention-based models concentrate on a single discriminative subsequence.
The recurrence of specific motifs (e.g., HIDRL, HQLLH, DEEVK) across multiple architectures suggests the models learn conserved biochemical features rather than arbitrary patterns.
The integration of XAI bridges computational performance with biological interpretability, showing that the networks capture molecular logic governing enzyme function.
future_direction: Extending the framework to multi-functional enzyme prediction.
Validating identified motifs against structural and biochemical databases to strengthen the connection between model explanations and experimentally verified protein function.
papers.abstract: Proteins perform essential biological functions, and accurate classification of their sequences is critical for understanding structure-function relationships, enzyme mechanisms, and molecular interactions. This study presents a deep learning-based framework for functional group classification of protein sequences derived from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). Four architectures were implemented: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM), CNN-BiLSTM hybrid, and CNN with Attention. Each model was trained using k-mer integer encoding to capture both local and long-range dependencies. Among these, the CNN achieved the highest validation accuracy of 91.8%, demonstrating the effectiveness of localized motif detection. Explainable AI techniques, including Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients, were applied to interpret model predictions and identify biologically meaningful sequence motifs. The discovered motifs, enriched in histidine, aspartate, glutamate, and lysine, represent amino acid residues commonly found in catalytic and metal-binding regions of transferase enzymes. These findings highlight that deep learning models can uncover functionally relevant biochemical signatures, bridging the gap between predictive accuracy and biological interpretability in protein sequence analysis.

papers.title: The geometry of BERT
papers.research_question: How does BERT's attention mechanism work internally, and what insights can be gained about its classification process?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a novel theoretical perspective on BERT's attention mechanism, introducing the concepts of directionality of subspace selection and cone index, and analyzes attention patterns and global information flow to understand its classification process.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into BERT's classification process, offering potential avenues for future architectural improvements in Transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
The attention mechanism in BERT performs a subspace selection driven by the searching engine process (Q, K, V matrices).
The self-attention matrix exhibits specific, classifiable patterns (e.g., directional gate, open gate, contextual gates) that convey different types of information.
The cone index and distribution analysis show that lower layers specialize in finding information content, while upper layers primarily propagate it.
The information content propagates globally as a mean information content; the MLP synthesizes information from different heads, breaking the channel structure.
Rank collapse in attention is reinterpreted as a potential carrier of directional information rather than a purely negative phenomenon.
future_direction: Analysis of the BERT learning process during training.
Examining the specialization of individual components in the BERT architecture.
Leveraging these findings to optimize the architecture of the Transformer encoder.
papers.abstract: Transformer neural networks, particularly Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), have shown remarkable performance across various tasks such as classification, text summarization, and question answering. However, their internal mechanisms remain mathematically obscure, highlighting the need for greater explainability and interpretability. In this direction, this paper investigates the internal mechanisms of BERT proposing a novel perspective on the attention mechanism of BERT from a theoretical perspective. The analysis encompasses both local and global network behavior. At the local level, the concept of directionality of subspace selection as well as a comprehensive study of the patterns emerging from the self-attention matrix are presented. Additionally, this work explores the semantic content of the information stream through data distribution analysis and global statistical measures including the novel concept of cone index. A case study on the classification of SARS-CoV-2 variants using RNA which resulted in a very high accuracy has been selected in order to observe these concepts in an application. The insights gained from this analysis contribute to a deeper understanding of BERT's classification process, offering potential avenues for future architectural improvements in Transformer models and further analysis in the training process.

papers.title: What Does BERT Look at? An Analysis of BERT’s Attention
papers.research_question: What specific linguistic features does BERT learn from unlabeled data, as revealed by its attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT's attention heads capture syntactic and coreference information, and proposes methods for analyzing attention mechanisms to reveal this linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Attention maps contain substantial linguistic knowledge and complement other model analysis techniques, and should be part of the toolkit for understanding what neural networks learn about language.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's attention heads exhibit common patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence.
Certain attention heads specialize to specific syntactic relations (e.g., direct objects, determiners) with high accuracy.
One attention head performs well at coreference resolution.
An attention-based probing classifier achieves 77 UAS on dependency parsing, showing BERT's attention captures substantial syntactic information.
Attention heads in the same layer tend to behave similarly.
papers.abstract: Large pre-trained neural networks such as BERT have had great recent success in NLP, motivating a growing body of research investigating what aspects of language they are able to learn from unlabeled data. Most recent analysis has focused on model outputs (e.g., language model surprisal) or internal vector representations (e.g., probing classifiers). Complementary to these works, we propose methods for analyzing the attention mechanisms of pre-trained models and apply them to BERT. BERT's attention heads exhibit patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence, with heads in the same layer often exhibiting similar behaviors. We further show that certain attention heads correspond well to linguistic notions of syntax and coreference. For example, we find heads that attend to the direct objects of verbs, determiners of nouns, objects of prepositions, and coreferent mentions with remarkably high accuracy. Lastly, we propose an attention-based probing classifier and use it to further demonstrate that substantial syntactic information is captured in BERT's attention.

papers.title: Priors in Time: Missing Inductive Biases for Language Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the temporal prior assumptions of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and how do they conflict with the actual temporal structure in language model activations? How can we design an interpretability method that incorporates appropriate temporal inductive biases?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Temporal Feature Analysis, a new interpretability protocol that decomposes language model activations into predictable (contextual) and novel (residual) components, capturing temporal structure that standard Sparse Autoencoders miss due to inappropriate inductive biases.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that interpretability tools must incorporate inductive biases that match the data's structure, and Temporal Feature Analysis offers a promising direction for capturing temporal dynamics in language model representations.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs impose an i.i.d. prior over time, assuming concepts are independent across time, which conflicts with the non-stationary temporal structure (e.g., increasing intrinsic dimensionality, context correlations) observed in language model activations.
Temporal Feature Analysis successfully decomposes activations into predictable (slow-moving, contextual) and novel (fast-moving, stimulus-driven) components, aligning with the generative structure of language.
The predictive component of Temporal Feature Analysis captures smooth temporal trajectories, event boundaries, and speaker roles in dialogue, while the novel component retains monosemantic features interpretable via standard autointerp pipelines.
In experiments on garden path sentences, stories, and in-context dialogue, Temporal Feature Analysis correctly parses linguistic structure and identifies event boundaries, whereas standard SAEs show significant pitfalls.
The method demonstrates that incorporating data-informed temporal inductive biases is crucial for robust interpretability tools.
papers.limitation: The method assumes that the residual novel component is i.i.d. over time, which may not hold in general.
future_direction: Explore other inductive biases (e.g., hierarchical, compositional) for interpretability.
Apply Temporal Feature Analysis to other modalities (e.g., video, audio).
Conduct more extensive causal intervention studies to validate the interpretability of the novel codes.
papers.abstract: Recovering meaningful concepts from language model activations is a central aim of interpretability. While existing feature extraction methods aim to identify concepts that are independent directions, it is unclear if this assumption can capture the rich temporal structure of language. Specifically, via a Bayesian lens, we demonstrate that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) impose priors that assume independence of concepts across time, implying stationarity. Meanwhile, language model representations exhibit rich temporal dynamics, including systematic growth in conceptual dimensionality, context-dependent correlations, and pronounced non-stationarity, in direct conflict with the priors of SAEs. Taking inspiration from computational neuroscience, we introduce a new interpretability objective -- Temporal Feature Analysis -- which possesses a temporal inductive bias to decompose representations at a given time into two parts: a predictable component, which can be inferred from the context, and a residual component, which captures novel information unexplained by the context. Temporal Feature Analyzers correctly parse garden path sentences, identify event boundaries, and more broadly delineate abstract, slow-moving information from novel, fast-moving information, while existing SAEs show significant pitfalls in all the above tasks. Overall, our results underscore the need for inductive biases that match the data in designing robust interpretability tools.

papers.title: Investigating the Encoding of Words in BERT's Neurons using Feature Textualization
papers.research_question: Can the knowledge encoded in individual neurons of BERT be interpreted and symbolized as words? How many neurons are needed to encode words in BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces feature textualization, an adaptation of activation maximization for language models, and uses it to show that single neurons in BERT do not encode words, but groups of 250-450 neurons do.
papers.conclusion: Feature textualization can retrieve interpretable synthetic inputs similar to words for well-chosen groups of neurons, but single neurons do not encode words.
papers.key_findings:
Single neurons in BERT do not encode words, as optimized inputs for single neurons are not semantically similar to word embeddings.
Words only utilize about 3% of the theoretical activation potential of single neurons on average.
For groups of 250-450 neurons, optimized inputs become similar to word embeddings, indicating words are encoded in distributed neuron clusters.
Feature textualization can reveal the information encoded in groups of neurons in language models.
The activation potential of individual neurons declines in higher layers of BERT.
papers.limitation:
The method is computationally expensive and infeasible for very large language models.
The interpretations are model-specific.
future_direction: Investigate the stability of findings with increased input length (contextualized words).
Apply the method to other language models, including those fine-tuned for downstream tasks or larger models.
Develop regularizers to pull optimized inputs towards the populated part of the word embedding space.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (PLMs) form the basis of most state-of-the-art NLP technologies. Nevertheless, they are essentially black boxes: Humans do not have a clear understanding of what knowledge is encoded in different parts of the models, especially in individual neurons. The situation is different in computer vision, where feature visualization provides a decompositional interpretability technique for neurons of vision models. Activation maximization is used to synthesize inherently interpretable visual representations of the information encoded in individual neurons. Our work is inspired by this but presents a cautionary tale on the interpretability of single neurons, based on the first large-scale attempt to adapt activation maximization to NLP, and, more specifically, large PLMs. We propose feature textualization, a technique to produce dense representations of neurons in the PLM word embedding space. We apply feature textualization to the BERT model (Devlin et al., 2019) to investigate whether the knowledge encoded in individual neurons can be interpreted and symbolized. We find that the produced representations can provide insights about the knowledge encoded in individual neurons, but that individual neurons do not represent clearcut symbolic units of language such as words. Additionally, we use feature textualization to investigate how many neurons are needed to encode words in BERT.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: Word Order Does Matter (And Shuffled Language Models Know It)
papers.research_question: Do shuffled language models still have traces of word order information? Why is there a gap in performance between models without position embeddings and models trained on shuffled tokens? Are there NLU benchmarks, other than GLUE, on which shuffled language models perform poorly?
papers.core_contribution: Shuffled language models retain word order information due to cues like adjacent BPE symbols and sentence length correlations, and word order is important for some NLU tasks beyond GLUE.
papers.conclusion: Shuffled language models retain word order knowledge largely at the local level due to cues like adjacent BPE symbols and sentence length correlations, and the order of shuffling (before or after BPE) influences this acquisition. Some NLU tasks are sensitive to word order.
papers.key_findings:
Shuffled language models contain substantial information about naturalistic word order, as shown by probing tasks.
The performance gap between models without position embeddings and shuffled models is due to position embeddings providing inductive bias and the presence of local n-grams when shuffling before BPE segmentation.
Even when shuffling after segmentation, models retain some word order information due to statistical dependencies between sentence length and unigram probabilities.
Attention patterns in shuffled models show a preference for adjacent tokens, mimicking convolutional windows.
Some NLU tasks (e.g., Winograd Schema, BoolQ, ReCoRD) are more sensitive to word order and show larger performance drops for shuffled models.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that language models pretrained and/or fine-tuned on randomly permuted sentences exhibit competitive performance on GLUE, putting into question the importance of word order information. Somewhat counter-intuitively, some of these studies also report that position embeddings appear to be crucial for models' good performance with shuffled text. We probe these language models for word order information and investigate what position embeddings learned from shuffled text encode, showing that these models retain information pertaining to the original, naturalistic word order. We show this is in part due to a subtlety in how shuffling is implemented in previous work -- before rather than after subword segmentation. Surprisingly, we find even Language models trained on text shuffled after subword segmentation retain some semblance of information about word order because of the statistical dependencies between sentence length and unigram probabilities. Finally, we show that beyond GLUE, a variety of language understanding tasks do require word order information, often to an extent that cannot be learned through fine-tuning.

papers.title: How does BERT’s attention change when you fine-tune? An analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope
papers.research_question: How does BERT's attention change when fine-tuned? The paper investigates this through a proposed analysis methodology and a case study in negation scope.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a methodology for testing hypotheses about how transformer models encode linguistic phenomena, using unsupervised probes, downstream control tasks, and cross-dataset consistency. Applying it to negation scope reveals evidence of the hypothesized encoding in base models but not in large models.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a procedure and analysis methods to test hypotheses about how transformer-based models encode linguistic phenomena. Applying this to negation scope finds evidence of an interpretable encoding (in-scope words attend to the negation cue) in BERT-base and RoBERTa-base, but weaker evidence in the large models.
papers.key_findings:
Before fine-tuning, several attention heads are sensitive to negation scope, with the best BERT-base head achieving an F1 of 53.8 in a fully unsupervised setting.
There is consistency in which heads are negation-sensitive across different datasets.
After fine-tuning on a negation scope task, the average sensitivity of attention heads improved over the pretrained model for all four models, but only the two base models improved more than a control task.
Attention heads that had the top F1s in the pretrained model do not have the top-ranked improvements after fine-tuning on negation scope.
The behavior of individual attention heads becomes more consistent across datasets after fine-tuning on the negation task, compared to the pretrained model and the control task, except for RoBERTa-large.
papers.limitation:
The work focuses on one interpretable way of encoding negation scope knowledge, but there could be many other ways.
The study uses a single nonlinguistic control task, but one could imagine exploring a gradient of fine-tuning tasks.
The analysis focuses primarily on the attention mechanism, but does not explore the value vectors that transformers apply the attention to.
future_direction: Explore other hypothesized encodings of negation scope, such as a tree of attention leading to the negation cue.
Explore attention head changes with a gradient of fine-tuning tasks that are more or less relevant to the linguistic phenomenon.
Explore the value vectors that transformers apply the attention to, since these form the outputs and are more directly tied to classification decisions.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models like BERT, after fine-tuning to a downstream task, have achieved high performance on a variety of NLP problems. Yet explaining their decisions is difficult despite recent work probing their internal representations. We propose a procedure and analysis methods that take a hypothesis of how a transformer-based model might encode a linguistic phenomenon, and test the validity of that hypothesis based on a comparison between knowledge-related downstream tasks with downstream control tasks, and measurement of cross-dataset consistency. We apply this methodology to test BERT and RoBERTa on a hypothesis that some attention heads will consistently attend from a word in negation scope to the negation cue. We find that after fine-tuning BERT and RoBERTa on a negation scope task, the average attention head improves its sensitivity to negation and its attention consistency across negation datasets compared to the pre-trained models. However, only the base models (not the large models) improve compared to a control task, indicating there is evidence for a shallow encoding of negation only in the base models.

papers.title: TopK Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we build a language model architecture that enjoys the interpretability of sparse autoencoders without suffering the drawbacks of post-hoc training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TopK LMs, a transformer-based language model architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function to achieve inherent, SAE-like interpretability without requiring post-hoc training, while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.conclusion: TopK LMs represent a significant advance toward trustworthy AI systems by making interpretability a built-in feature, demonstrating that performance and interpretability need not be competing objectives.
papers.key_findings:
TopK LMs achieve competitive language modeling and downstream task performance compared to dense baselines, with only a moderate increase in model size.
Neurons in TopK LMs exhibit higher concept specialization, as measured by lower token and semantic entropy, making them more interpretable.
Single-neuron interventions (activation patching) can causally steer the model's text generation towards specific concepts.
The formation and specialization of individual neurons can be traced continuously across training checkpoints and model layers.
Sparsity annealing during training improves convergence and model performance.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on models up to ~1B parameters; effectiveness on significantly larger models remains an open question.
Evaluation focused on language modeling and standard reasoning benchmarks, leaving performance on specialized downstream tasks unclear.
Long-context modeling capabilities and the interaction between TopK sparsity and attention over long sequences were not examined.
The approach is currently limited to text-only models; extending to multimodal architectures requires future research.
Specific societal applications that could benefit from the model's interpretability were not explored.
future_direction: Scaling the TopK LM approach to significantly larger models (tens or hundreds of billions of parameters).
Extending TopK activation to multimodal architectures combining text with images, audio, or other modalities.
Investigating how TopK LMs can address concrete challenges in model alignment, fairness assessment, safety evaluation, and trustworthy AI deployment.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an important tool for analyzing and interpreting the activation space of transformer-based language models (LMs). However, SAEs suffer several shortcomings that diminish their utility and internal validity. Since SAEs are trained post-hoc, it is unclear if the failure to discover a particular concept is a failure on the SAE's side or due to the underlying LM not representing this concept. This problem is exacerbated by training conditions and architecture choices affecting which features an SAE learns. When tracing how LMs learn concepts during training, the lack of feature stability also makes it difficult to compare SAEs features across different checkpoints. To address these limitations, we introduce a modification to the transformer architecture that incorporates a TopK activation function at chosen layers, making the model's hidden states equivalent to the latent features of a TopK SAE. This approach eliminates the need for post-hoc training while providing interpretability comparable to SAEs. The resulting TopK LMs offer a favorable trade-off between model size, computational efficiency, and interpretability. Despite this simple architectural change, TopK LMs maintain their original capabilities while providing robust interpretability benefits. Our experiments demonstrate that the sparse representations learned by TopK LMs enable successful steering through targeted neuron interventions and facilitate detailed analysis of neuron formation processes across checkpoints and layers. These features make TopK LMs stable and reliable tools for understanding how language models learn and represent concepts, which we believe will significantly advance future research on model interpretability and controllability.

papers.title: Multilingual Chart-based Constituency Parse Extraction from Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we extract constituency parses from pre-trained language models without training, and can this be done effectively across multiple languages?
