papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a chart-based method and a top-K ensemble technique for extracting constituency parses from pre-trained language models without training, and demonstrates that multilingual PLMs enable effective parsing across multiple languages.
papers.conclusion: The chart-based method and top-K ensemble improve constituency parse extraction from PLMs, and multilingual PLMs enable effective parsing across multiple languages, providing a foundation for unsupervised parsing for under-represented languages and probing multilingual PLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Chart-based methods (CP and CC) outperform the top-down method (TD) in most cases.
The top-K ensemble technique significantly improves parsing performance.
Multilingual PLMs can be used for constituency parse extraction across multiple languages, achieving performance comparable or superior to unsupervised PCFGs.
The method is robust to cross-lingual transfer, with minimal performance loss when using attention heads selected for English on other languages.
There exist universal attention heads that are sensitive to syntactic information across languages.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on a validation set for hyperparameter selection (attention head selection), so it is not entirely unsupervised.
The performance, while competitive, still falls short of standard supervised parsers.
The chart parsing algorithm has O(n^3) time complexity, which is less efficient than top-down parsing.
future_direction: Developing a method that is free from validation set annotations.
Designing an ensemble method that gathers information from heterogeneous PLMs.
Thorough analysis of the effect of parsing strategies across languages.
papers.abstract: As it has been unveiled that pre-trained language models (PLMs) are to some extent capable of recognizing syntactic concepts in natural language, much effort has been made to develop a method for extracting complete (binary) parses from PLMs without training separate parsers. We improve upon this paradigm by proposing a novel chart-based method and an effective top-K ensemble technique. Moreover, we demonstrate that we can broaden the scope of application of the approach into multilingual settings. Specifically, we show that by applying our method on multilingual PLMs, it becomes possible to induce non-trivial parses for sentences from nine languages in an integrated and language-agnostic manner, attaining performance superior or comparable to that of unsupervised PCFGs. We also verify that our approach is robust to cross-lingual transfer. Finally, we provide analyses on the inner workings of our method. For instance, we discover universal attention heads which are consistently sensitive to syntactic information irrespective of the input language.

papers.title: Interpretability with full complexity by constraining feature information
papers.research_question: How can we achieve interpretability in machine learning without sacrificing model complexity by constraining the information about input features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for interpretability that constrains the information flow from each input feature without restricting model complexity, using the Distributed Information Bottleneck, providing a continuum of feature importance and fine-grained inspection of feature effects.
papers.conclusion: The Distributed Information Bottleneck provides a novel source of interpretability by illuminating where information resides in the input features, without sacrificing model complexity.
papers.key_findings:
The method can identify the features and feature values most important for prediction by analyzing the optimal information allocation.
It allows full complexity of feature processing and interactions, compatible with arbitrary neural network architectures.
It provides a learned continuum of feature inclusion-to-exclusion and fine-grained compression schemes for each feature.
The method is intuitive to implement with minimal additional overhead, training a single model while sweeping the information bottleneck strength.
It demonstrates utility on a range of tabular datasets, providing interpretability signals comparable to or exceeding other methods.
papers.abstract: Interpretability is a pressing issue for machine learning. Common approaches to interpretable machine learning constrain interactions between features of the input, rendering the effects of those features on a model's output comprehensible but at the expense of model complexity. We approach interpretability from a new angle: constrain the information about the features without restricting the complexity of the model. Borrowing from information theory, we use the Distributed Information Bottleneck to find optimal compressions of each feature that maximally preserve information about the output. The learned information allocation, by feature and by feature value, provides rich opportunities for interpretation, particularly in problems with many features and complex feature interactions. The central object of analysis is not a single trained model, but rather a spectrum of models serving as approximations that leverage variable amounts of information about the inputs. Information is allocated to features by their relevance to the output, thereby solving the problem of feature selection by constructing a learned continuum of feature inclusion-to-exclusion. The optimal compression of each feature -- at every stage of approximation -- allows fine-grained inspection of the distinctions among feature values that are most impactful for prediction. We develop a framework for extracting insight from the spectrum of approximate models and demonstrate its utility on a range of tabular datasets.

papers.title: Disentangling Neuron Representations with Concept Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we find meaningful directions (concept vectors) in activation space that correspond to distinct features, starting from polysemantic neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors that represent distinct features, allowing for fine-grained concept separation controlled by a distance threshold.
papers.conclusion: Exploring directions in activation space (concept vectors) instead of individual neurons can lead to finding coherent fundamental units, bridging mechanistic interpretability and concept discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into concept vectors that are linear combinations of neurons.
The concept vectors encode coherent, human-understandable features, as validated by human experiments.
The method can separate fine-grained concepts (e.g., underwater scenes vs. scuba divers) by adjusting a distance threshold.
The latent space representations have higher similarity with the discovered concept vectors than with the neuron directions.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the data used to generate clusters.
All experiments were performed on image data, which may limit generalizability to other data types.
future_direction: Generalizing the method to other data types such as language and tabular data.
Looking at other starting candidates for concepts besides neurons.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how models store representations by breaking down neural networks into interpretable units. However, the occurrence of polysemantic neurons, or neurons that respond to multiple unrelated features, makes interpreting individual neurons challenging. This has led to the search for meaningful vectors, known as concept vectors, in activation space instead of individual neurons. The main contribution of this paper is a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors encapsulating distinct features. Our method can search for fine-grained concepts according to the user’s desired level of concept separation. The analysis shows that polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into directions consisting of linear combinations of neurons. Our evaluations show that the concept vectors found encode coherent, human-understandable features.

papers.title: The Mythos of Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the motivations for interpretability in machine learning, and what properties or techniques are thought to confer interpretability to models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a critical analysis of the concept of interpretability in machine learning, arguing that the term is ill-defined and encompasses diverse and sometimes conflicting motivations and notions, and that claims about interpretability must be qualified with specific definitions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the machine learning community must critically engage with the problem formulation of interpretability, and that researchers and practitioners share responsibility for ensuring machine learning aligns with societal desiderata.
papers.key_findings:
Linear models are not strictly more interpretable than deep neural networks; the validity of such a claim depends on the specific notion of interpretability being used (e.g., algorithmic transparency vs. decomposability).
Claims about interpretability must be qualified by specifying the definition of interpretability being employed, as the term refers to multiple distinct concepts.
In some cases, the desire for model transparency may conflict with broader objectives of AI, such as achieving higher predictive performance.
Post-hoc interpretations can potentially mislead, especially if they are optimized to produce plausible but unfaithful explanations.
The demand for interpretability often arises from a mismatch between formal machine learning objectives (e.g., test set performance) and real-world deployment costs or desiderata.
future_direction: Developing richer loss functions and performance metrics to mitigate the discrepancy between real-life and machine learning objectives.
Expanding the analysis of interpretability to other machine learning paradigms such as reinforcement learning.
Addressing challenges like fairness and contestability in the context of interpretability.
papers.abstract: In machine learning, the concept of interpretability is both important and slippery.

papers.title: Challenges in Mechanistically Interpreting Model Representations
papers.research_question: What are the challenges in mechanistically interpreting model representations, and how do current mechanistic interpretability tools fall short in understanding complex behaviors like dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the importance of studying feature and behavior representations in models, performs an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in Mistral-7B, and shows that current mechanistic interpretability tools are insufficient for understanding such representations, advocating for new frameworks.
papers.conclusion: Studying representations for features and behaviors is crucial for understanding models, but current mechanistic interpretability tooling is inadequate for answering key questions about representations, necessitating new frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations for dishonesty can be found and used to steer model behavior, but they are not simply boosting generically dishonest tokens.
Continual injections of the dishonesty direction are required for open-ended dishonest generation, not just at the first token.
Direct logit attribution shows that directional injections affect many components, with MLPs having a more direct effect than attention heads.
Activation patching reveals that many components are involved in the dishonesty behavior, making sparse circuit analysis difficult and less helpful.
Current mechanistic interpretability tooling (e.g., patching) is insufficient for understanding how representations are formed and how they affect long-term generation.
papers.limitation: Patching methods (activation and path patching) do not rigorously prove that circuits found are indeed reserved to that task, and patching only one component at a time might not isolate components if multiple perform the same job.
future_direction: Study how different components interact with representations and alter them.
Explore the training dynamics of a model and study the emergence of representations as a model trains.
Develop new frameworks to think about and study representations.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to understand AI models by reverse-engineering the exact algorithms neural networks learn. Most works in MI so far have studied behaviors and capabilities that are trivial and token-aligned. However, most capabilities important for safety and trust are not that trivial, which advocates for the study of hidden representations inside these networks as the unit of analysis. We formalize representations for features and behaviors, highlight their importance and evaluation, and perform an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1'. We justify that studying representations is an important and under-studied field, and highlight several challenges that arise while attempting to do so through currently established methods in MI, showing their insufficiency and advocating work on new frameworks for the same.

papers.title: Analyzing Feed-Forward Blocks in Transformers through the Lens of Attention Maps
papers.research_question: How do feed-forward blocks in transformers modify input contextualization, and how do their effects interact with surrounding components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes feed-forward blocks in transformers and shows that they modify input contextualization to emphasize specific linguistic compositions, and that their effects are often canceled by surrounding residual and normalization layers, suggesting redundancy.
papers.conclusion: FF blocks in transformers modify input contextualization to emphasize linguistic compositions, but their effects are often canceled by surrounding components, suggesting redundancy in the transformer's internal processing.
papers.key_findings:
FF networks modify input contextualization, with larger changes in specific layers (e.g., middle to late layers in BERT, early layers in GPT-2).
FF amplifies specific types of linguistic compositions, such as subwords-to-word and words-to-multi-word-expression constructions.
The effects of FF are often canceled by subsequent residual and normalization layers, indicating redundancy in the transformer layer.
The cancellation is due to the large norm of the residual bypass vector and the shrinking of outlier dimensions by layer normalization.
The contextualization changes are not simply explained by word co-occurrence (low correlation with PMI).
papers.limitation: The method is computationally costly for large models and long inputs, making it challenging to apply to billion-scale LLMs.
future_direction: Lightening the computational cost of the method.
Experimenting with other datasets and models.
Investigating the cause of differences between BERT and GPT-2 in FF effects.
papers.abstract: Transformers are ubiquitous in wide tasks. Interpreting their internals is a pivotal goal. Nevertheless, their particular components, feed-forward (FF) blocks, have typically been less analyzed despite their substantial parameter amounts. We analyze the input contextualization effects of FF blocks by rendering them in the attention maps as a human-friendly visualization scheme. Our experiments with both masked- and causal-language models reveal that FF networks modify the input contextualization to emphasize specific types of linguistic compositions. In addition, FF and its surrounding components tend to cancel out each other's effects, suggesting potential redundancy in the processing of the Transformer layer.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How can lexical semantic knowledge be extracted from pretrained language models, how is this knowledge distributed across layers, and how do the extracted representations compare to traditional static word embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic study of how to extract type-level lexical semantic knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that monolingual models store rich lexical information primarily in lower layers and that extracted vectors can outperform traditional word embeddings on several monolingual tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effectively uncovering this knowledge depends on careful configuration of extraction strategies, with universal best practices including using monolingual LMs, encoding words with multiple contexts, excluding special tokens, and averaging over lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantic knowledge is concentrated in the lower Transformer layers of pretrained language models.
Averaging representations across multiple layers yields better performance than using a single layer.
Monolingual language models contain more lexical information for a target language than massively multilingual models like mBERT.
Extracted 'BERT-based' static word embeddings outperform fastText on monolingual tasks (e.g., lexical similarity, analogy, relation prediction) but not on cross-lingual tasks (BLI, CLIR).
Translation pairs obtain similar representations in independently trained monolingual LMs, indicating approximate isomorphism between the monolingual spaces.
papers.limitation: The comparison with fastText word embeddings is not strictly apples-to-apples because the models were trained on different corpora (Wikipedia dumps for fastText vs. the corpora used for pretraining the LMs).
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect the extraction of word representations and how to sample representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, more lexical semantic probes, and other larger underlying language models.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods, such as layer weighting or attention, and lightweight methods to enrich lexical content in multilingual LMs.
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-ofcontext versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: Feature Importance Estimation with Self-Attention Networks
papers.research_question: Can attention-based neural networks be used for feature importance estimation in tabular data, and how do they compare to established feature ranking methods?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Self-Attention Networks (SANs) for feature importance estimation in tabular data, showing they perform competitively with established methods and can capture feature interactions.
papers.conclusion: SANs are a viable method for feature importance estimation in tabular data, comparable to existing methods, and can capture feature interactions.
papers.key_findings:
SANs identify similar high-ranked features as established feature ranking methods (ReliefF, Mutual Information, Random Forest).
SANs can detect feature interactions which in some cases yield better predictive performance than baselines.
The attention mechanism in SANs can be used to estimate feature importance directly from the model.
SANs have high space complexity (O(|F|^2) per attention head) which may be a drawback for very high-dimensional data.
On smaller datasets, SANs may not perform as well due to insufficient data for the attention mechanism to distill relevant features.
papers.limitation:
SANs have high space complexity (O(|F|^2) per attention head), which could be prohibitive for very high-dimensional data without sparsity.
SANs may not perform well on small datasets due to insufficient data for the attention mechanism to learn relevant features.
future_direction: Exploring sparsity to reduce the space complexity of SANs.
Comparing SANs with the recently introduced TabNet.
papers.abstract: Black-box neural network models are widely used in industry and science, yet are hard to understand and interpret. Recently, the attention mechanism was introduced, offering insights into the inner workings of neural language models. This paper explores the use of attention-based neural networks mechanism for estimating feature importance, as means for explaining the models learned from propositional (tabular) data. Feature importance estimates, assessed by the proposed Self-Attention Network (SAN) architecture, are compared with the established ReliefF, Mutual Information and Random Forest-based estimates, which are widely used in practice for model interpretation. For the first time we conduct scale-free comparisons of feature importance estimates across algorithms on ten real and synthetic data sets to study the similarities and differences of the resulting feature importance estimates, showing that SANs identify similar high-ranked features as the other methods. We demonstrate that SANs identify feature interactions which in some cases yield better predictive performance than the baselines, suggesting that attention extends beyond interactions of just a few key features and detects larger feature subsets relevant for the considered learning task.

papers.title: Understanding polysemanticity in neural networks through coding theory
papers.research_question: How can coding theory and eigenspectrum analysis provide insights into polysemanticity and improve interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a coding theory perspective to neural network interpretability, using eigenspectrum analysis of activation covariance and random projections to understand polysemanticity, redundancy, and the trade-off between capacity and robustness in network codes.
papers.conclusion: The eigenspectrum analysis and random projections offer a top-down perspective on neural network interpretability, advancing understanding of code structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks learn codes that balance capacity and redundancy, with eigenspectrum decay indicating the level of redundancy.
Dropout during training leads to faster eigenspectrum decay, more robust codes, and smoother random projections.
Random projections of hidden activations reveal the smoothness of the code, which is linked to eigenspectrum decay and can complement single-neuron interpretability methods.
In large language models, random projections provide explanatory power in layers where single-neuron methods perform poorly, suggesting complementary approaches.
The framework explains polysemanticity as an efficient encoding strategy and provides theoretical insights into optimal coding and error correction.
papers.limitation: Identifying the exact error-correcting code is beyond the scope of this paper.
future_direction: A systematic study of how eigenspectrum decay changes with network size.
Investigating the role of nonlinearities in the network code.
Further research into the underlying structure and behavior of deep learning models from a coding perspective.
papers.abstract: Despite substantial efforts, neural network interpretability remains an elusive goal, with previous research failing to provide succinct explanations of most single neurons' impact on the network output. This limitation is due to the polysemantic nature of most neurons, whereby a given neuron is involved in multiple unrelated network states, complicating the interpretation of that neuron. In this paper, we apply tools developed in neuroscience and information theory to propose both a novel practical approach to network interpretability and theoretical insights into polysemanticity and the density of codes. We infer levels of redundancy in the network's code by inspecting the eigenspectrum of the activation's covariance matrix. Furthermore, we show how random projections can reveal whether a network exhibits a smooth or non-differentiable code and hence how interpretable the code is. This same framework explains the advantages of polysemantic neurons to learning performance and explains trends found in recent results by Elhage et al.~(2022). Our approach advances the pursuit of interpretability in neural networks, providing insights into their underlying structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: Transformer Key-Value Memories Are Nearly as Interpretable as Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: To what extent does a proxy-based, artificial decomposition of neuron activations (e.g., via sparse autoencoders) empirically benefit model interpretation compared to the organic features already represented within the original model's feed-forward layers?
papers.core_contribution: Features from feed-forward key-value memories (FF-KV) are nearly as interpretable as those from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and in some aspects (e.g., absorption, explained variance) even outperform SAEs, suggesting that FF-KV features serve as a strong baseline for interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Proxy-based methods such as SAEs offer very limited empirical advantage over direct analysis of feed-forward layers, and FF-KV features should be included as a strong baseline in interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FF-KV features achieve comparable interpretability to SAE features across multiple automatic evaluation metrics from SAEBENCH.
FF-KV features sometimes outperform SAEs, e.g., in absorption (less redundancy) and explained variance (perfect by definition).
Human evaluation shows conceptual features can be found with almost equal ease from both FF-KV and SAEs.
Features discovered by proxy methods (e.g., Transcoders) often do not align with features in the original FF module, suggesting potential hallucination.
Increasing sparsity in FF-KV (via TopK) does not consistently improve interpretability across metrics.
papers.limitation:
SCR and TPP scores are highly unstable and should be treated as supplementary results.
The theoretical advantage of SAEs is not observed empirically through the current evaluation scheme.
future_direction: Further research on the faithfulness of learned features from proxy modules, with FF-KV features as grounding points.
Inclusion of FF-KV features as a baseline when assessing feature-discovery methods in interpretability.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability work on large language models (LLMs) has been increasingly dominated by a feature-discovery approach with the help of proxy modules. Then, the quality of features learned by, e.g., sparse auto-encoders (SAEs), is evaluated. This paradigm naturally raises a critical question: do such learned features have better properties than those already represented within the original model parameters, and unfortunately, only a few studies have made such comparisons systematically so far. In this work, we revisit the interpretability of feature vectors stored in feed-forward (FF) layers, given the perspective of FF as key-value memories, with modern interpretability benchmarks. Our extensive evaluation revealed that SAE and FFs exhibits a similar range of interpretability, although SAEs displayed an observable but minimal improvement in some aspects. Furthermore, in certain aspects, surprisingly, even vanilla FFs yielded better interpretability than the SAEs, and features discovered in SAEs and FFs diverged. These bring questions about the advantage of SAEs from both perspectives of feature quality and faithfulness, compared to directly interpreting FF feature vectors, and FF key-value parameters serve as a strong baseline in modern interpretability research.

papers.title: The Dead Salmons of AI Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the failure modes and statistical fragilities of contemporary AI interpretability methods, and how can they be addressed through a statistical-causal reframing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues for a statistical-causal reframing of AI interpretability, where explanations are treated as parameters of a statistical model inferred from computational traces, to address false discoveries and statistical fragility.
papers.conclusion: Situating interpretability within the standard toolkit of statistical inference opens promising avenues for turning AI interpretability into a pragmatic and rigorous science.
papers.key_findings:
Many interpretability methods (feature attribution, probing, sparse autoencoders, circuit discovery) produce plausible-looking explanations even when applied to randomly initialized neural networks, demonstrating 'dead salmon' artifacts.
Interpretability methods suffer from broader statistical fragility, including poor generalization, high variance, and sensitivity to experimental design choices.
The root cause of these issues is the non-identifiability of many interpretability queries, meaning computational traces do not uniquely determine explanations.
Hypothesis testing against randomized null models (e.g., comparing a trained network to a randomly initialized one) can mitigate dead salmon artifacts, as shown in probing experiments.
A formal statistical-causal framework, where explanations are surrogate models answering distributions of causal queries, provides a principled foundation for evaluating and improving interpretability methods.
future_direction: Active selection of queries to reduce uncertainty
Meta-analysis of interpretability studies
Bayesian uncertainty quantification for explanations
papers.abstract: In a striking neuroscience study, the authors placed a dead salmon in an MRI scanner and showed it images of humans in social situations. Astonishingly, standard analyses of the time reported brain regions predictive of social emotions. The explanation, of course, was not supernatural cognition but a cautionary tale about misapplied statistical inference. In AI interpretability, reports of similar ''dead salmon'' artifacts abound: feature attribution, probing, sparse auto-encoding, and even causal analyses can produce plausible-looking explanations for randomly initialized neural networks. In this work, we examine this phenomenon and argue for a pragmatic statistical-causal reframing: explanations of computational systems should be treated as parameters of a (statistical) model, inferred from computational traces. This perspective goes beyond simply measuring statistical variability of explanations due to finite sampling of input data; interpretability methods become statistical estimators, and findings should be tested against explicit and meaningful alternative computational hypotheses, with uncertainty quantified with respect to the postulated statistical model. It also highlights important theoretical issues, such as the identifiability of common interpretability queries, which we argue is critical to understand the field's susceptibility to false discoveries, poor generalizability, and high variance. More broadly, situating interpretability within the standard toolkit of statistical inference opens promising avenues for future work aimed at turning AI interpretability into a pragmatic and rigorous science.

papers.title: Enhancing Automated Interpretability with Output-Centric Feature Descriptions
papers.research_question: How can we generate faithful feature descriptions for LLMs by considering both the inputs that activate a feature and its causal effect on model outputs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes efficient, output-centric methods (VocabProj and TokenChange) for automatically generating feature descriptions in LLMs, and demonstrates that combining these with input-centric methods yields the most faithful descriptions across both input and output evaluations.
papers.conclusion: Output-centric methods provide efficient and effective ways to generate feature descriptions that capture causal effects, and their combination with input-centric methods yields more faithful and complete descriptions, enhancing automated interpretability pipelines.
papers.key_findings:
Output-centric feature descriptions (VocabProj, TokenChange) better capture the causal effect of a feature on model outputs than the prevalent input-centric method (MaxAct).
Combining input- and output-centric methods (ensembles) leads to the best performance on both input- and output-based evaluations of description faithfulness.
Output-centric methods are computationally efficient, requiring only a few inference passes, and can serve as a cheap alternative to MaxAct in some cases.
Output-centric descriptions can be used to find inputs that activate 'dead' features for which no activating inputs were previously identified.
Performance varies by layer and feature type, with output-based performance being lower for MLP features compared to residual stream features.
papers.abstract: Automated interpretability pipelines generate natural language descriptions for the concepts represented by features in large language models (LLMs), such as plants or the first word in a sentence. These descriptions are derived using inputs that activate the feature, which may be a dimension or a direction in the model's representation space. However, identifying activating inputs is costly, and the mechanistic role of a feature in model behavior is determined both by how inputs cause a feature to activate and by how feature activation affects outputs. Using steering evaluations, we reveal that current pipelines provide descriptions that fail to capture the causal effect of the feature on outputs. To fix this, we propose efficient, output-centric methods for automatically generating feature descriptions. These methods use the tokens weighted higher after feature stimulation or the highest weight tokens after applying the vocabulary "unembedding" head directly to the feature. Our output-centric descriptions better capture the causal effect of a feature on model outputs than input-centric descriptions, but combining the two leads to the best performance on both input and output evaluations. Lastly, we show that output-centric descriptions can be used to find inputs that activate features previously thought to be "dead".

papers.title: On the Interpretability of Attention Networks
papers.research_question: How can we quantitatively measure the interpretability of attention models? Also, under what conditions are attention models accurate but not interpretable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Selective Dependence Classification (SDC) task and the Focus-Classify Attention Model (FCAM) to objectively measure interpretability of attention networks, identifies error modes where attention models are accurate but not interpretable, and shows that sparsity-inducing methods can improve interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The SDC task and FCAM provide a framework for objectively measuring interpretability in attention models, and sparsity can help improve interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Attention models can be accurate but not interpretable, with three identified error modes: the focus model mistakes one foreground class as background, the focus and classification models are individually poor but together accurate, and the classification network is powerful enough to classify even with a poor focus model.
Sparsity-inducing methods such as sparsemax and spherical softmax can improve interpretability (FT) without sacrificing accuracy.
Using later layers of the focus network for averaging the attended input can improve interpretability compared to using the input layer.
papers.limitation: The SDC task is cartoon-like and unrealistic for real data, as it assumes full label dependence on a single foreground segment and independence of background segments.
future_direction: Investigating other error modes under which accurate attention models are non-interpretable.
Extending the framework to more complex tasks and real-world data.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms form a core component of several successful deep learning architectures, and are based on one key idea: ''The output depends only on a small (but unknown) segment of the input.'' In several practical applications like image captioning and language translation, this is mostly true. In trained models with an attention mechanism, the outputs of an intermediate module that encodes the segment of input responsible for the output is often used as a way to peek into the `reasoning` of the network. We make such a notion more precise for a variant of the classification problem that we term selective dependence classification (SDC) when used with attention model architectures. Under such a setting, we demonstrate various error modes where an attention model can be accurate but fail to be interpretable, and show that such models do occur as a result of training. We illustrate various situations that can accentuate and mitigate this behaviour. Finally, we use our objective definition of interpretability for SDC tasks to evaluate a few attention model learning algorithms designed to encourage sparsity and demonstrate that these algorithms help improve interpretability.

papers.title: Warp: a method for neural network interpretability applied to gene expression profiles
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be interpreted in the context of gene expression analysis to recover meaningful information on a sample-specific basis?
papers.core_contribution: Warping is a method for neural network interpretability that recovers sample-specific gene signatures by interpolating in input or representation space, demonstrating effectiveness on linearly and non-linearly separable datasets.
papers.conclusion: Warping shows promise as a flexible method for post-hoc interpretation of neural networks in computational biology, enabling the examination of class gene signatures with sample-specific insights.
papers.key_findings:
Warping works well on non-linearly separable datasets like XOR, allowing data points to migrate across decision boundaries.
The method provides sample-specific bias vectors, highlighting individual adjustments needed for classification changes.
In a VAE-based approach, warping recovers biologically meaningful gene expression adjustments, such as suppressing surfactant genes and boosting kidney-specific genes to change phenotype classification.
papers.limitation:
Linear interpolation assumes the data manifold is continuous in input space, which may lead to adversarial examples.
Reconstruction blurriness caused by the variational autoencoder encoding.
future_direction: Determine how destructive warps are to other gene signatures within samples.
Overcome reconstruction blurriness caused by the VAE encoding.
papers.abstract: We show a proof of principle for warping, a method to interpret the inner working of neural networks in the context of gene expression analysis. Warping is an efficient way to gain insight to the inner workings of neural nets and make them more interpretable. We demonstrate the ability of warping to recover meaningful information for a given class on a samplespecific individual basis. We found warping works well in both linearly and nonlinearly separable datasets. These encouraging results show that warping has a potential to be the answer to neural networks interpretability in computational biology.

papers.title: DoLFIn: Distributions over Latent Features for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we achieve interpretability in neural models without sacrificing accuracy by using probability distributions over latent features?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DoLFIn, a novel architecture for interpretability that uses probability distributions over latent features, and shows it achieves comparable or better accuracy than baselines while providing interpretability.
papers.conclusion: DoLFIn provides a new way to build explainable models without sacrificing accuracy, and it offers better interpretability than attention and saliency maps.
papers.key_findings:
DoLFIn achieves slightly higher accuracy than CNN and BiLSTM on SST2 and AG-news datasets.
DoLFIn provides interpretability by computing the probability that an input word supports a category, which is more informative than attention or saliency maps.
The latent features in DoLFIn can be analyzed to understand which categories they support, and some features are more specific to certain categories.
papers.limitation: The analysis of the meaning of latent features is only done on a cherry-picked example and deeper analysis is left for future work.
future_direction: Deeply analyzing the meaning of latent features.
papers.abstract: Interpreting the inner workings of neural models is a key step in ensuring the robustness and trustworthiness of the models, but work on neural network interpretability typically faces a trade-off: either the models are too constrained to be very useful, or the solutions found by the models are too complex to interpret. We propose a novel strategy for achieving interpretability that -- in our experiments -- avoids this trade-off. Our approach builds on the success of using probability as the central quantity, such as for instance within the attention mechanism. In our architecture, DoLFIn (Distributions over Latent Features for Interpretability), we do no determine beforehand what each feature represents, and features go altogether into an unordered set. Each feature has an associated probability ranging from 0 to 1, weighing its importance for further processing. We show that, unlike attention and saliency map approaches, this set-up makes it straight-forward to compute the probability with which an input component supports the decision the neural model makes. To demonstrate the usefulness of the approach, we apply DoLFIn to text classification, and show that DoLFIn not only provides interpretable solutions, but even slightly outperforms the classical CNN and BiLSTM text classifiers on the SST2 and AG-news datasets.

papers.title: DGTN: Graph-Enhanced Transformer with Diffusive Attention Gating Mechanism for Enzyme DDG Prediction
papers.research_question: How can we accurately predict the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (∆∆G) by integrating sequence and structural information through a co-learning framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DGTN, a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network and transformer representations through a bidirectional diffusion mechanism for protein stability prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: DGTN effectively integrates 3D geometric and evolutionary sequence context through bidirectional diffusion, establishing a principled and interpretable paradigm for accurate protein stability prediction and design.
papers.key_findings:
DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance on ProTherm with Pearson correlation ρ=0.87 and RMSE=1.21 kcal/mol, outperforming existing baselines.
Ablation studies show the bidirectional diffusion mechanism contributes a 6-point gain in Pearson correlation over simple cross-modal fusion.
The model generalizes well to unseen datasets (SKEMPI, Ssym, FireProtDB), demonstrating robust learning of stability principles.
Theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to an optimal structure-aware attention matrix with a convergence rate of O(1/√T).
Attention visualization confirms the model successfully identifies spatially proximate but sequentially distant residue interactions.
papers.limitation:
Operates on a single static conformation of the wild-type protein, unable to capture dynamic or entropic contributions to stability.
Evaluates mutations in isolation and does not explicitly model epistatic (non-additive) interactions between multiple substitutions.
Training data (ProTherm) exhibits class imbalance, with certain protein families overrepresented, potentially limiting generalization.
future_direction: Incorporate ensembles of structures (from molecular dynamics or predicted distributions) to model flexibility and allostery.
Extend the architecture to jointly represent combinatorial mutations via graph-based mutation encoding or interaction-aware attention.
Improve robustness to dataset imbalance via domain-adversarial training, balanced sampling, or cross-family transfer learning.
papers.abstract: Predicting the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (DDG) is fundamental to protein engineering and drug design. While recent deep learning approaches have shown promise, they often process sequence and structure information independently, failing to capture the intricate coupling between local structural geometry and global sequential patterns. We present DGTN (Diffused Graph-Transformer Network), a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network (GNN) weights for structural priors and transformer attention through a diffusion mechanism. Our key innovation is a bidirectional diffusion process where: (1) GNN-derived structural embeddings guide transformer attention via learnable diffusion kernels, and (2) transformer representations refine GNN message passing through attention-modulated graph updates. We provide rigorous mathematical analysis showing this co-learning scheme achieves provably better approximation bounds than independent processing. On ProTherm and SKEMPI benchmarks, DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance (Pearson Rho = 0.87, RMSE = 1.21 kcal/mol), with 6.2% improvement over best baselines. Ablation studies confirm the diffusion mechanism contributes 4.8 points to correlation. Our theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to optimal structure-sequence coupling, with convergence rate O(1/sqrt(T) ) where T is diffusion steps. This work establishes a principled framework for integrating heterogeneous protein representations through learnable diffusion.

papers.title: Interpretability in Linear Brain Decoding
papers.research_question: What is a formal definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models, and how can we quantitatively evaluate interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a formal definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models and proposes a multi-objective criterion combining interpretability and performance for model selection.
papers.conclusion: The proposed definition provides a theoretical background for the quantitative evaluation of interpretability in linear brain decoding.
papers.key_findings:
In noisy data, the most accurate linear decoding model is not necessarily the most interpretable, highlighting a trade-off between performance and interpretability.
Incorporating the proposed interpretability measure into model selection can lead to more interpretable models when using regularization techniques like Lasso.
papers.limitation:
The definition of interpretability is theoretical and assumes the true solution of the brain decoding problem is available, which is not realistic in practice.
The definition and quantification are limited to linear models; extending to non-linear models requires future research.
future_direction: Extending the definition of interpretability to non-linear models.
papers.abstract: Improving the interpretability of brain decoding approaches is of primary interest in many neuroimaging studies. Despite extensive studies of this type, at present, there is no formal definition for interpretability of brain decoding models. As a consequence, there is no quantitative measure for evaluating the interpretability of different brain decoding methods. In this paper, we present a simple definition for interpretability of linear brain decoding models. Then, we propose to combine the interpretability and the performance of the brain decoding into a new multi-objective criterion for model selection. Our preliminary results on the toy data show that optimizing the hyper-parameters of the regularized linear classifier based on the proposed criterion results in more informative linear models. The presented definition provides the theoretical background for quantitative evaluation of interpretability in linear brain decoding.

papers.title: T3-Vis: visual analytic for Training and fine-Tuning Transformers in NLP
papers.research_question: How can we design a visual analytic framework to assist researchers in understanding and interpreting the training and fine-tuning processes of Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents T3-Vis, a visual analytic framework that integrates multiple interactive visualizations to help researchers understand and interpret the training and fine-tuning of Transformer models by providing insights into hidden states, attention patterns, and training dynamics.
papers.conclusion: T3-Vis is an effective framework for interpreting Transformer models during training and fine-tuning, and it helps identify potential directions to improve task performance.
papers.key_findings:
In extractive summarization, important attention heads exhibit patterns where tokens attend to other tokens of the same word, tokens within the same sentence, and adjacent tokens.
In topic classification, the framework helped identify misclassified examples and revealed that the model sometimes focuses on unimportant details or fails when background knowledge is required.
The framework was found useful by researchers in a focus group for interpreting model behavior and identifying potential improvements.
papers.limitation:
The interface is more useful for classification problems with well-defined evaluation metrics.
There is information loss intrinsic in the dimension reduction methods used for visualization.
The front-end needs optimization to support visualization of large-scale datasets.
future_direction: Extend the framework to provide more advanced visualization for custom Transformers, such as models with more complex connections (e.g., parallel attention layers) or advanced attention mechanisms (e.g., sparse attention).
papers.abstract: Transformers are the dominant architecture in NLP, but their training and fine-tuning is still very challenging. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of a visual analytic framework for assisting researchers in such process, by providing them with valuable insights about the model's intrinsic properties and behaviours. Our framework offers an intuitive overview that allows the user to explore different facets of the model (e.g., hidden states, attention) through interactive visualization, and allows a suite of built-in algorithms that compute the importance of model components and different parts of the input sequence. Case studies and feedback from a user focus group indicate that the framework is useful, and suggest several improvements. Our framework is available at:

papers.title: Effective Attention Sheds Light On Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does effective attention provide different interpretations than standard attention for transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Effective attention, which contributes to model output, reveals different interpretations than standard attention, being less focused on delimiter tokens and more on task-relevant linguistic features.
papers.conclusion: Effective attention should be used for interpreting transformers as it is more pertinent to model output and reveals task-relevant features.
papers.key_findings:
Effective attention shows fewer vertical patterns associated with delimiter tokens compared to standard attention.
Effective attention disregards [SEP] and punctuation tokens but not [CLS].
Effective attention highlights end-task linguistic features instead of pretraining-related features.
Changes in attention due to fine-tuning are captured by effective attention, confirming its relevance to model output.
Effective attention is more pertinent for interpreting transformer behavior as it directly contributes to the output.
papers.limitation: Effective attention is slower to compute due to the SVD decomposition, which can be a bottleneck for large-scale analyses.
future_direction: A more formal study comparing norm-based analysis and effective attention.
papers.abstract: An attention matrix of a transformer selfattention sublayer can provably be decomposed into two components and only one of them (effective attention) contributes to the model output. This leads us to ask whether visualizing effective attention gives different conclusions than interpretation of standard attention. Using a subset of the GLUE tasks and BERT, we carry out an analysis to compare the two attention matrices, and show that their interpretations differ. Effective attention is less associated with the features related to the language modeling pretraining such as the separator token, and it has more potential to illustrate linguistic features captured by the model for solving the end-task. Given the found differences, we recommend using effective attention for studying a transformer's behavior since it is more pertinent to the model output by design.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformers Models
papers.research_question: How to interactively explore and understand what attention heads in transformer models have learned, specifically in BERT, by combining attention visualization with nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to explore and explain learned representations and attention mechanisms in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to reveal intelligible structure in learned representations of transformer models, demonstrated with BERT on the Wizard of Oz corpus.
papers.key_findings:
At early layers (e.g., layer 1), masked token embeddings show similarity to common tokens like punctuation and determinants, with no meaningful linguistic information encoded.
As layers progress, more part-of-speech information is added; by layer 6, BERT becomes confident that a masked token is a verb, refining this estimation in later layers.
Complex dependencies such as direct object (DOBJ) are detected in early-middle layers but rely on a combination of multiple attention heads, not individual heads.
Positional heads attend to succeeding or preceding tokens and encode linguistic information about the attended-to word, such as part-of-speech and dependency relations.
EXBERT enables interactive exploration of how attention heads contribute to encoding linguistic features in token embeddings through nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce powerful contextual representations that lead to improvements across many NLP tasks. Since these models are typically guided by a sequence of learned self attention mechanisms and may comprise undesired inductive biases, it is paramount to be able to explore what the attention has learned. While static analyses of these models lead to targeted insights, interactive tools are more dynamic and can help humans better gain an intuition for the model-internal reasoning process. We present exBERT, an interactive tool named after the popular BERT language model, that provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations by matching a human-specified input to similar contexts in a large annotated dataset. By aggregating the annotations of the matching similar contexts, exBERT helps intuitively explain what each attention-head has learned.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: From Neurons to Neutrons: A Case Study in Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability extract scientific knowledge from neural networks trained on physics data, and can such insights align with human-derived domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can extract scientifically meaningful representations from neural networks trained on nuclear physics data, aligning with human-derived concepts like the semi-empirical mass formula and shell model.
papers.conclusion: These findings provide a proof-of-concept that neural networks, when trained on scientific data, can learn useful representations that align with human knowledge, opening exciting possibilities for future research on richer data and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings of proton and neutron numbers exhibit a helix structure that encodes nuclear physics concepts like the volume and asymmetry terms.
The orderedness of embeddings along the first principal component correlates with generalization performance.
Penultimate layer features correspond to terms in the semi-empirical mass formula and nuclear shell model.
Latent space topography reveals the algorithm used by the model for binding energy prediction, geometrically representing the SEMF.
Models trained on nuclear data learn representations similar to those trained on pseudo data from human-derived theory.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted knowledge is not guaranteed; representations may be complex and not easily distilled into interpretable theories.
Lack of quantitative metrics to assess interpretability.
Symbolic regression from neural features did not yield fully interpretable improvements over human-derived models.
Requires interdisciplinary collaborations and close partnerships between machine learning researchers and domain experts.
future_direction: Applying interpretability to richer data and more complex tasks.
Developing quantitative metrics for interpretability.
Exploring other scientific domains for knowledge extraction.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) promises a path toward fully understanding how neural networks make their predictions. Prior work demonstrates that even when trained to perform simple arithmetic, models can implement a variety of algorithms (sometimes concurrently) depending on initialization and hyperparameters. Does this mean neuron-level interpretability techniques have limited applicability? We argue that high-dimensional neural networks can learn low-dimensional representations of their training data that are useful beyond simply making good predictions. Such representations can be understood through the mechanistic interpretability lens and provide insights that are surprisingly faithful to human-derived domain knowledge. This indicates that such approaches to interpretability can be useful for deriving a new understanding of a problem from models trained to solve it. As a case study, we extract nuclear physics concepts by studying models trained to reproduce nuclear data.

papers.title: Decomposing MLP Activations into Interpretable Features via Semi-Nonnegative Matrix Factorization
papers.research_question: How can we find interpretable features in large language models by decomposing MLP activations using semi-nonnegative matrix factorization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SNMF for decomposing MLP activations into interpretable features, outperforming SAEs and supervised baselines in causal steering, and reveals hierarchical structure in MLP activation space.
papers.conclusion: SNMF is a simple and effective tool for identifying interpretable features and dissecting concept representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SNMF-derived features outperform SAEs and a supervised baseline (difference-in-means) on causal steering.
SNMF features align with human-interpretable concepts and show good concept detection.
Recursive SNMF reveals hierarchical merging of features, e.g., fine-grained concepts into high-level ones.
Specific neuron combinations are reused across semantically-related features.
MLP features are compositional and exhibit a parts-based decomposition.
papers.limitation: A minority of MLP features receive negative scores, indicating they respond more strongly to neutral contexts, possibly reflecting sensitivity to noise or layer-specific biases.
future_direction: Optimizations for SNMF initialization and training
papers.abstract: A central goal for mechanistic interpretability has been to identify the right units of analysis in large language models (LLMs) that causally explain their outputs. While early work focused on individual neurons, evidence that neurons often encode multiple concepts has motivated a shift toward analyzing directions in activation space. A key question is how to find directions that capture interpretable features in an unsupervised manner. Current methods rely on dictionary learning with sparse autoencoders (SAEs), commonly trained over residual stream activations to learn directions from scratch. However, SAEs often struggle in causal evaluations and lack intrinsic interpretability, as their learning is not explicitly tied to the computations of the model. Here, we tackle these limitations by directly decomposing MLP activations with semi-nonnegative matrix factorization (SNMF), such that the learned features are (a) sparse linear combinations of co-activated neurons, and (b) mapped to their activating inputs, making them directly interpretable. Experiments on Llama 3.1, Gemma 2 and GPT-2 show that SNMF derived features outperform SAEs and a strong supervised baseline (difference-in-means) on causal steering, while aligning with human-interpretable concepts. Further analysis reveals that specific neuron combinations are reused across semantically-related features, exposing a hierarchical structure in the MLP's activation space. Together, these results position SNMF as a simple and effective tool for identifying interpretable features and dissecting concept representations in LLMs.

papers.title: Probing for Predicate Argument Structures in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: Do pretrained language models (PLMs) encode the argument structure of a predicate in its contextual representation? How are predicate senses and their argument structures encoded across layers, and how do they differ between verbal and nominal predicates and across languages?
papers.core_contribution: PLMs encode predicate argument structures in their contextual representations, with senses and rolesets encoded at different layers, and verbal and nominal predicates are represented differently. Integrating this knowledge improves SRL performance.
papers.conclusion: Probing PLMs for predicate argument structures reveals how they encode semantic information and provides insights that can be used to improve SRL systems.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs encode predicate argument structures directly into the contextualized representation of a predicate.
Predicate senses and their argument structures are encoded at different layers in PLMs.
Verbal and nominal predicate argument structures are represented differently across the layers of a PLM, making transfer between them non-trivial.
Multilingual PLMs encode predicate argument structure information similarly across English and Chinese.
Integrating predicate-argument structure knowledge into an SRL model via weighted averaging of layers and multi-task learning improves performance.
future_direction: cross-lingual transfer learning for SRL
using all layers of PLMs for SRL
papers.abstract: Thanks to the effectiveness and wide availability of modern pretrained language models (PLMs), recently proposed approaches have achieved remarkable results in dependencyand span-based, multilingual and cross-lingual Semantic Role Labeling (SRL). These results have prompted researchers to investigate the inner workings of modern PLMs with the aim of understanding how, where, and to what extent they encode information about SRL. In this paper, we follow this line of research and probe for predicate argument structures in PLMs. Our study shows that PLMs do encode semantic structures directly into the contextualized representation of a predicate, and also provides insights into the correlation between predicate senses and their structures, the degree of transferability between nominal and verbal structures, and how such structures are encoded across languages. Finally, we look at the practical implications of such insights and demonstrate the benefits of embedding predicate argument structure information into an SRL model.

papers.title: Enhancing Pre-trained Representation Classifiability can Boost its Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can classifiability-oriented pre-trained representations achieve high interpretability and classifiability simultaneously?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a positive correlation between interpretability and classifiability in pre-trained vision representations, introduces the Inherent Interpretability Score (IIS) to quantify representation interpretability, and shows that improving one can mutually promote the other.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability and classifiability are mutually promoting for classifiability-oriented pre-trained representations, allowing practitioners to unify improvements in both aspects for vision models.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability and classifiability of pre-trained representations are positively correlated, not conflicting.
